subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF REGRET AND SYMPATHY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DEATH OF FORMER MEMBER FOR DAVENPORT
subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF REGRET AND SYMPATHY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I realize that it is not customary to refer to the passing of persons who were formerly members of this house. However, in a few cases exceptions should be made, and I believe the sudden death of John R. MacNicol, the former member for Davenport, should be one of those cases.
I was shocked to learn of Mr. MacNicol's passing. For the last few months we have been corresponding with respect to a project which was very dear to him, and as a matter of fact I was in the process of acknowledging a letter he had written me only last Friday when I heard of his death. As I am sure all hon. members will agree, for many years Mr. MacNicol was a beloved and revered figure in this house. He was first elected as a Conservative in 1930, and was re-elected continuously until the general election of 1949. I suppose Mr. MacNicol was one of the most travelled members of parliament. When the house was not in session he was usually off to acquaint himself with various parts of our country and learn of the problems of those living in other provinces and territories. As a result of his travels he acquired a vast store of knowledge on matters relating to irrigation and the development of our resources generally, which he put to very good use on his return to the house.
It can be said of Mr. MacNicol, I think, that at least among members of parliament he counted none but friends. Those who knew him were struck by his kind and gentle manner, by his good nature, and by his sense of service not only to his own constituents of Davenport but to all Canadians everywhere.
On behalf of my colleagues on this side of the house I should like to express to the leader of the party to which Mr. MacNicol belonged our sincere sympathy.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: DEATH OF FORMER MEMBER FOR DAVENPORT
subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF REGRET AND SYMPATHY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is a fitting tribute to our late friend John R. MacNicol that the Prime Minister (Mr. St.
Laurent) should have varied the ordinary custom to indicate the regret felt in every part of the house, as in every part of Canada, at the passing of a truly great Canadian.
In many ways John R. MacNicol was a unique figure. He was extremely loyal to the party in which he believed and of which he was a member; he had served that party in its highest offices, but in his untiring efforts to advance the best interests of this country he continued to make recommendations for the development of our resources, the conservation of our soil, and so on, only in the hope that the dominion government, the provincial governments or the municipal governments concerned, without regard to political point of view, might carry out the plans in which he believed.
As the Prime Minister has said, of those members who knew him over the years each one was a friend. Mr. MacNicol was untiring in his efforts to encourage recognition of the possibilities of increasing the productive capacity of our country, by reclamation, by conservation, by irrigation in western Canada, by power development in the maritime provinces, and generally by the development of our great resources.
Mr. MacNicol was always proud of Toronto. He never failed to express his pride in what Toronto was to him, and what he believed it would be in the years ahead. But he was equally anxious at all times to serve every part of this country. As has already been stated, between sessions he visited every part of Canada in an effort to encourage the furthering of those plans in which he believed. He will be greatly missed by all who knew him, and by Canadians everywhere who were encouraged by his bright vision of the future. While certainly not a young man at the time of his passing, that vision and the prospects ahead had never been dimmed; his eyes were always on that bright horizon.

Mr. Speaker, I join with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) in expressing regret at the passing of Mr. MacNicol. The seating arrangements in parliament threw us together, and for two parliaments we sat side by side. I got to know Mr. MacNicol well. Each session we looked forward to the report that he would make of his travels during the recess. Speaking as one who represents a prairie

MacNicol constituency, I know that I express the appreciation of the people in Alberta and Saskatchewan, perhaps Saskatchewan particularly, for the great interest he took in the welfare of the communities adjacent to the great rivers, and his untiring efforts on behalf of the irrigation plans that have been discussed over the years.
Mr. MacNicol lived a full life. I sometimes think there is much to be thankful for when a man lives a full life, as he did, and passes as he passed. Spared a long period of illness, in the full vigour of his intellect, and deeply interested, as the Prime Minister has indicated, in the schemes which he supported, he has passed to his reward. It recalls to all of us that ancient phrasing of the Book of Common Prayer, "In the midst of life we are in death".
Mr. Solon, E. Low (Peace River):	Mr. Speaker, we should like to associate ourselves with the tributes that have been paid to the late Mr. MacNicol, and to express our sincere regret at his sudden passing. We learned to love and admire the fine qualities of this great man. We in the west particularly were grateful to him for the way in which he interpreted the east to the west and the west to the east; and he contributed greatly to national and international understanding and good will.
We believe that Mr. MacNicol was instrumental in inducing much development in the west. He was one of the few men I knew who really understood how important it was that the west be developed. He recognized how important its development would be as a market for eastern manufacturers, and he spent a great deal of time trying to establish various types of works in, the west that would help us to get the type of development we needed. We loved him for what he was- a sincere, honourable, fine gentleman.

maintopic: DEATH OF FORMER MEMBER FOR DAVENPORT
subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF REGRET AND SYMPATHY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the tributes paid to the memory of Mr. John Ritchie MacNicol were fitting and well deserved. I knew him well and liked him. He was an excellent member of parliament, spending his time during the session either in the house or in his office getting information for his summer travels. He was more than a traveller; he was an explorer and prospector. He never missed an opportunity to improve his knowledge about Canada, his beloved country; and he never missed an occasion to help anyone. As one of his colleagues, I remember many instances of his political courage; he was most useful in his own way. I cannot forget it. He was scholarly and well informed. He was endowed with a high degree of public spirit, and


his career was useful not only to his constituents, not only to the city of Toronto which he loved, not only to the province of Ontario, but to the whole country. Whenever he had a practical suggestion to make, he looked so happy. He looked happier only when he had support for his suggestion.
Sir, I must say that although some of our political beliefs were different, we were very good friends, just as I was with the late Tommy Church, who was a close friend of Mr. MacNicol. Tommy used to call Mr. MacNicol "John R.," and so did I. John R. used to call Mr. Church "Tommy", as we all did. They were fine men; they represent the glorious past of the Conservative party.
Mr. MacNicol has occupied high positions in the party. If I recall aright, he was president of the dominion Conservative association, and presided over one of the conventions that selected a leader. He saw to it that there was a fine book published with the names and pictures of all the delegates. He gave me one.
May I be permitted to recall one incident in particular when Mr. MacNicol helped me a great deal. It was during the difficult sessions of the civil service committee. I had some difficulty with my Conservative colleagues who wanted some information to be considered confidential. I spoke of it to someone who spoke to somebody else, and the somebody else spoke to Mr. MacNicol, who saw the leader of his party. Things were arranged so that we could get the information required, but it took a lot of good will and good disposition. Mr. MacNicol was always there whenever he was needed to give a hand to his colleagues.
I must recall to hon. members that his family and Mr. Mackenzie King's family were very close friends, and tributes were paid to Mr. MacNicol in the house by the former prime minister. I cannot do otherwise than tell my leader that I am delighted that he has paid such a fine tribute to the memory of a great member of parliament and a great Canadian. I congratulate the leader of the opposition, the leader of the C.C.F. group (Mr. Coldwell) and the leader of the Social Credit group (Mr. Low) for having also spoken so well about a beloved colleague who has just passed to the great beyond.

maintopic: DEATH OF FORMER MEMBER FOR DAVENPORT
subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF REGRET AND SYMPATHY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the hon. member for Dan-forth (Mr. Harris) and the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Hellyer) I wish to pay tribute to the former member for Davenport, whom I knew in this house and outside of it as a most kindly gentleman. He was a man of wide interests, extending far beyond his own constituency, and of great attainments,

which he displayed in the house on many occasions. To me he exemplified true Cana-dianism. He was greatly respected throughout the country, and was particularly loved in the city of Toronto. I am sure the house will agree with me that he will be missed in the Canadian scene. His passing is a matter of personal loss to the people of the city of Toronto. He will be particularly missed there.

maintopic: DEATH OF FORMER MEMBER FOR DAVENPORT
subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF REGRET AND SYMPATHY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a backbencher may I concur in everything that has been said by those who have preceded me in paying tribute to a great Canadian. The late John R. MacNicol was always a booster for the development of our natural resources, both in the east and in the west; but he was particularly interested in irrigation projects in Alberta.
In the passing of Mr. MacNicol we in southeastern Alberta have lost a great eastern booster for the development of our irrigation projects. He will be sadly missed by every one of us in that area; but his memory will be cherished and will give us added strength to carry on where he has left off, until our dreams are realized and we shall have water flowing over more of the dry areas of the western plains.
May I extend to his relatives my deepest sympathy.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. G. F. Higgins (St. John's East):
subtopic: GRAND BANKS
speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries. Is the minister aware of conditions on the grand banks of Newfoundland, in that trawlers of foreign nations are causing damage to property and endangering the lives of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia fishermen fishing there? If so, will the minister outline what he proposes to do in the matter? What is the result of the recent visit to Newfoundland of the special investigators sent by the department?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. W. Mayhew (Minister of Fisheries):
subtopic: GRAND BANKS
speechtext:
The hon. member for St. John's East followed his usual practice and sent me notice of his question, which is appreciated. We are aware of the problems in this area. The area itself is international waters, and control would require an international agreement among the various countries.
We are asking the captains of the Canadian fishing vessels to keep records and give us
3784	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways
evidence of any destruction of or interference with the Canadian fishing gear. Further, we intend to discuss the problem with European countries this fall when our representative goes to Europe on other busi-iness, so that we might ultimately have a conference on the rules of the road in the northwest Atlantic. We are also sending our largest vessel, the Cygnus, into that area to give what protection we can to the Canadian fishermen and also to their vessels, but I might point out that the vessel is not going as a policeman; it is going to render assistance.
The hon. member's second question was:
What is the result of the recent visit to Newfoundland of the special investigators sent by the department?
The representatives returned from Newfoundland a few days ago and have prepared their report. They first submitted it to the fisheries prices support board. I have received it verbally, but not officially. The committee met on Friday, and again on Saturday. I think they will be making a full report today. This report will then go to my colleagues for consideration, along with my recommendation, and when it has been dealt with by cabinet, will be presented in due course.
The trawler policy of the government was outlined in the statement that I made some time ago and has not been changed to date.

speechtext:
This is the clause giving authority to vote money to meet so-called deficits in connection with current revenues. Before proceeding with what I rose to say may I make it clear that I support this bill, and I do so for two reasons. On the one hand I feel that the Canadian National is encumbered with a capital structure that makes these deficits inevitable, and therefore we have no option but to meet them. The other point is that the Canadian National, as the national railway, is called upon to give service in a good many parts of the country where it is not a profit-making operation.

Since we call upon the Canadian National to do that, we have no alternative but to pay any deficits that arise therefrom. However, when parliament is called upon to vote these sums of money, or to give authority to vote them, as is the case under section 9, it does seem to me that our questions as to the ways in which the money is spent should be answered in parliament.
I have in mind a great many questions I have asked about pensions, special allowances in lieu of pensions, and special lump sum allowances to employees of the Canadian National. In all cases but one my questions have been answered. I am grateful for the extensive information I have been given in relation to this matter. It makes it possible for me to point out the large number of Canadian National employees in receipt of pensions that are far too low, concerning which the Canadian National should do something soon. But it does seem farcical that the authorities should be prepared to answer one after another all the questions to which I shall make reference in a moment, and then give a blank with respect to one particular question.
Let me give a small amount of detail. On March 22 of this year, as reported at page 997 of Hansard, I was given specific details as to the number of employees contributing to various plans, and more particularly as to the number of retired employees drawing pensions in the brackets I indicated in my question, starting with less than $25 per month and going right up to $99.99 per month. The number in the lower brackets is really startling. In addition I asked for the number drawing pensions of $100 or more per month, and I was given the figure of 9,855. Later, on April 24, as recorded at page 1806 of Hansard, I was given a breakdown of those drawing pensions of more than $100 per month. I asked for them in various brackets going right up to $499.99 per month, and also the number drawing pensions of $500 or more per month. In all cases my questions were answered without hesitation. In the same set of questions on April 24 I went on to ask the number of retired employees in receipt of retirement allowances, including pensions from any pension plans plus supplementary allowances totalling various amounts, starting with $100 per month and going up to $500 per month or over, and again I was given the information. I find there are only eight people drawing regular pensions which include allowances supplementary to whatever pensions they may have earned. Those eight include four in the bracket between $100 and $200 per month, three in the bracket between $200 and $300 per month, and one in the bracket 55946-2401
Canadian National Railways between $400 and $500 per month. In those cases, of course, what I was asking about had to do with regular pension payments which are received month by month or quarter by quarter, as the case may be.
I emphasize that up to this point there was no difficulty. Whatever questions I asked about pensions or special allowances were answered just as soon as the government could get the information from the Canadian National Railways. Then I moved along and on May 15, as recorded at page 2517 of Hansard, I asked further questions about special retirement allowances. In particular I asked this question:
How many employees or officials of the Canadian National Railways, upon retirement, have been given lump sum retirement allowances (a) of $5,000 or less; (b) more than $5,000 but not more than $25,000, since January 1, 1930?
The answer to those questions was "none". I believe that is a correct answer; I am told there have been no lump sum retirement allowances in those amounts. The main point is that I got an answer. That information was given me in addition to all the detailed information I have referred to at these various pages of Hansard as to pensions and regular supplementary allowances paid to various retired employees. Well, it seemed to me only logical, since I was given all that information, that I should go a step higher.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I must confess I am a little interested to know how the member for Winnipeg North Centre could anticipate our views, and I am wholly unaware of the differences in his mind with regard to some of the aspects of this matter. Be that as it may, I do not think the minister has correctly interpreted this section. I do not believe he has intentionally misled the house, but there are features of it which he has overlooked.
This section provides that the government may make the advances required by Canadian National Railways, and then the last part of the section provides that all such amounts shall be reimbursed to the Minister of Finance from the annual revenues of the national railway system, in so far as such revenues are sufficient, and any insufficiency shall be provided for by a subsequent deficit appropriation by parliament. I am not arguing one way or the other as to the desirability of providing for the money in this way, but I do want to emphasize what the effect is. May I say, in regard to a remark which I heard at the time the member for Winnipeg North Centre was speaking, that we are taking up a lot of time on this bill, that we are dealing with something here that is likely to involve over $40 million. I think the members of this house should know exactly what they are doing.
As to whether that amount should or should not be provided, I do not think there is going to be any debate. Certainly the amount that will be contributed by this parliament subsequently will include all items of expenditure, whatever they may be. This bill is not merely permissive legislation which allows the advance to be made, which advances then are to be reimbursed to such extent as they can be reimbursed out of revenues of the railway. It goes further, it says that any insufficiency shall be provided for by a subsequent deficit appropriation by parliament. It does not say "may"; consequently any subsequent discretionary authority of parliament is removed by the passing of this section in its present form.

The minister says that this is subsequently dealt with by a vote. He has overlooked the fact that parliament now decides that any deficit, whatever it may be, shall be paid. This becomes statutory authority for the figure approved by the auditors which is included in the subsequent vote. It is not only dealt with by parliament, but it is authorized by parliament in what is now done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
The Canadian National Railways start off each year with the deficit you are now talking about. It is a fixed interest charge on old defunct railroads that should have been put into liquidation. In the second place, $21 million a year is paid back by the Canadian National to the Canadian government, in interest on loans that they make for refinancing purpose. The assertion that the government for beneficent reasons each year pays the deficit that accumulates to the Canadian National is wrong and misleading.
I like to be fair and honest about these things. The Canadian National had no deficit last year. You are not wiping out a deficit. You are paying interest charges of $24 million a year on bonds of old defunct railroads that produce no revenue. You can perhaps justify that because they are performing some service in communities where the C.P.R. would not operate. That $21 million interest earned by the money that we vote in this house goes back to the Canadian government in fixed interest charges. I think we should be clear about the fact that the railroad is not operating at a deficit.
I do not want to discuss this matter at length. It is before a commission now. The C. N. R. president is emphatic about a revision of the whole capital structure of the Canadian National Railways. I do not like to hear the Minister of Finance referring to this bill as one that is designed to wipe off a deficit of the Canadian National Railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: He did not.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Because they did not have a deficit. They inherited the mess they have, and I hope that Mr. Gordon will get the co-operation of the members of this house in cleaning up that historic mess which they inherited and for which they are not responsible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for trying to clear up a point that I had tried to clear up, namely, that this is not a bill to cover operating deficits of the Canadian National Railways. It is a bill to authorize advances to Canadian National Railways, first, for an approved capital program, second, if needed, to authorize temporary advances to cover an operating deficit. That is all the bill is for. I do not suppose the committee expects me at this time to enter into a discussion of recapitalization, if that is desirable, of the Canadian National Railways.
It is a question which is an extremely involved one, as the committee knows, entail-


ing a great many considerations. I really would not want to embark on that discussion at this time.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: You could not explain it before lunch.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS

I should like to make one comment. I think we all agree that there is a question of first-class importance here, that is to say, what burden should be carried by the management of the Canadian National Railways. On the one hand it is obviously unfair that they should be saddled with a deficit or a burden from the past which really makes their operating position impossible for the future. On the other hand, certain relief has been given in the past.
I think the matter is before a commission now and it seems to me that it is a matter which is going to require great judgment and discernment. Actually the idea that the Canadian National Railways operating position is greatly worse than that of other railways does not stand the test if you compare it with that of some perfectly good railways in the United States. I say that for this reason: I am sympathetic to the management of the Canadian National Railways, but on the other hand I think discretion must be shown in dealing with this question.
I want to ask the minister a question with regard to the wording at the beginning of clause 9. I will ask him to follow it with me as I read slowly the first three lines, because they seem to me to present a rather curious result.
Has the minister the wording of clause 9 before him?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
The first three lines read as follows:
If at any time before the first day of July, nineteen hundred and fifty-one, the available revenues of the national railway system are not sufficient to pay all the operating and income charges of the system . . .
And so on. The next section I think makes perfectly clear what I think is obvious, that it is the annual revenue that is referred to there; that is to say, it is the revenue for 1950. Does the minister agree with that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Quite right.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Then what is the reason for the time lag? Does the minister agree that, as it is worded now, if you take it alone, if anyone came along, not knowing anything about the background of this matter, I am not at all sure that he would read the words "the available revenues of the national railway system" as meaning only for the year 1950.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: I am glad my hon. friend raised that question. The purpose of that wording is this. In previous bills the date has been March 31 of the current year. The committee will realize that because the sessional committee rarely sits before March or April, it is not possible to bring this bill in until usually the end of May, or sometimes late in June. It thereby becomes effective for a period of only eight or nine months if March 31 is used. Therefore the date of July 1 was used, in order to give the legislation, so far as may be practicable, a full twelve months operation. That is the explanation. That applies only to the current advances; of course the July 1, 1951, does not relate to the capital advances referred to in subsection 2.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Does the minister agree that the words "the available revenues of the national railway system," in order to be perfectly clear should be followed by the words "during the year 1950"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: This is enabling power. If the C.N.R., on the current basis, is short of cash to pay its operating charges at a given point, whether it is in the middle of the year or at any other time, then this section operates and the government makes temporary advances. And once a year, as I have indicated and as the leader of the opposition has underlined, we come to parliament and get a specific vote for the deficit in the particular year. But the moneys are advanced, if necessary, from month to month out of the consolidated revenue fund.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Let us assume that in the first months of the year, say in 1950, the Canadian National Railways had an operating deficit-if I may use that unpleasant expression-of $25 million. Let us assume for the sake of argument that in the first three months of the year 1951 they had a tremendous run of luck and had an operating surplus of $25 million. Would they use that to cancel out the deficit of the year before? In other words, are we merging the two years in the matter of accounting?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
No, we are not merging the two years in the matter of accounting. Perhaps I could illustrate the matter in this way. Suppose in the month of May, 1951, by reason of operating conditions, the Canadian National Railways were running a substantial revenue deficit and needed money. The only way they could get it would be to borrow from the government. The date that is put in this section is to enable such advances to be made. My hon. friend will recall that last year I suggested, because it seemed to me to be more sensible, an open-ended period, subject to the requirements of the deficit that
Canadian National Railways had to be voted. That did not commend itself to the views of the committee. I do not quarrel with that; but what I have been trying to do is to provide a period of approximately twelve months during which this section will be operative. There is no intention to merge, nor do I consider that the language of the section permits any merging of, the accounts of the railways over two periods.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Does this bill not merely set up a sort of letter of credit for the railways on which they can draw until the vote is made in the next session of parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Subject to the approval of the Minister of Transport and the governor in council, that is correct.

Section agreed to.
On section 10-When revenue of Trans-Canada Air Lines and subsidiaries insufficient to meet operating and income charges.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
Clause 10 is the one which provides for the advances of money to Trans-Canada Air Lines and the subsequent appropriation by parliament of any deficit which may result during the following year.
As I pointed out in connection with the previous clause, which relates to the Canadian National Railways, this is not merely a provision which permits the government, with the authorization of parliament, to advance moneys to the Canadian National Railways as they are required for their operation; it also establishes-, as a decision of this parliament at this time, that whatever the deficiency may be as a result of these operations parliament shall-not "may"-by subsequent deficit appropriation meet that amount. Since that is so, this is an appropriate point at which to examine the whole situation with which we are confronted, and to indicate that every step should be taken to make that deficit as small as possible by every practical device that can be adopted.
While this is a bill presented by the Minister of Finance, it is presented through him on behalf of the government to deal with these governmental operations. Since the government is responsible for the broad problem, that problem should be examined in relation to the authorization now given, so -that any considerations affecting steps that may be taken by the government between now and the next session to reduce to the ultimate deficit may be placed before parliament and the government at this time.
I think it is time-in fact the time is overdue-for parliament to review carefully the events that have -taken place in connection with the Trans-Canada Air Lines. I hope that in making the comments I do we shall

Canadian National Railways not be confronted with the specious suggestion that an attempt to approach the problems of Trans-Canada Air Lines on a businesslike basis implies criticism of the line or of those who operate it. That device has been employed too often in an attempt to divert discussion which should be directed to the operation of many of these great enterprises, which can carry on only with the approval of parliament, and which parliament should certainly examine most carefully.
I think it would be well, when we remember that Trans-Canada Air Lines had by far the largest deficit in its history during this past year, to review the basis upon which parliament approved the setting up of this line. In introducing and discussing on March 22, 1937, the bill dealing with this organization, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce had this to say, as recorded at page 2043 of Hansard of that year:
It is thought that from the start the mail contract and such passenger and express business as is immediately available should cover the cost of the services. We have made provision, however, for a subsidy to protect the service in that period. After 1940, as I have said, the. subsidy provision expires and the mail contract will be on the basis of cost of the service. I think that outlines fairly well the intention of the bill. The whole matter can be more fully considered when the bill is brought down.
These words are simple, understandable, and not open to any misinterpretation. This operation was to maintain itself from its revenues, and after-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the leader of opposition. Does he think that on this clause he can go into the history of Trans-Canada Air Lines and explain why such deficits have to be met now? It seems to me that on clause 10, to be strictly relevant, what should be discussed is whether or not the deficit is to be met in the manner indicated in clause 10; there should not be any explanation of deficits. I should like to hear the leader of the opposition on that point.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
Yes, I think it is strictly relevant to the provisions of this section. Parliament is being asked to provide the money required for the operation of this line. This house is asked to approve a section which says that any deficit resulting at the end of the year shall be met by parliamentary appropriation. What I am pointing out is that it is desirable to review the situation so that when the government is dealing with this subject, provided that the house authorizes this, as there is every indication it will, the authorization shall be accompanied with proposed suggestions which they should consider to the end that the deficit may be reduced as much as possible. I am simply reviewing the situation which has developed from that point to the

present for the purpose of indicating things that could and should be done so that this deficit may be as small as possible. There is no other place that I am aware of where proper consideration could be given to these points.
In Hansard of June 24,1940, we find on page 1050 of the budget the following item under Trans-Canada Air Lines:
The operation of the Trans-Canada Air Lines expanded greatly during the calendar year 1939. Operating revenue increased from $591,000 to $2,350,000. The annual deficit, after payment of interest on capital and depreciation, decreased from $818,000 in 1938 to $412,000 in 1939.
That seemed to be in accord with the general pattern that had been projected by the minister who proposed this bill. In 1941, as reported at page 1743 of Hansard of March 20, the Minister of Trade and Commerce had this to say:
Last year the earnings of the air lines, after all write-offs and interest on investment, were something over $500,000. This year it is anticipated that the earnings from air mail based on the increased mileage and the 40-cent rate will be $3,153,000. The passenger revenue will be $2,170,000. Miscellaneous revenue, comprised chiefly of express, will amount to $250,000, giving a total gross revenue of $5,573,500. Operating expenses are anticipated to be $5,315,477, giving an operating income of $258,032, less interest on capital, and other income charges, of $197,500. That leaves us with an estimated surplus of $60,523.
Actually in the years that followed a surplus was built up. Therefore up to that point the pattern that had been projected by the Minister of Trade and Commerce was being followed. Then the pattern changed. We have had a succession of deficits which first of all wiped out the accumulated surplus, and last year reached $4,317,593. I submit that when the House of Commons is asked to pass a section authorizing advances to any of the public bodies brought into existence by the parliament of Canada it is appropriate to examine the assurances given at the time and to see whether we have or have not departed from that basis. If we have, then we should find out what can be done to limit the deficit which, by this very section, parliament now says will be met by a subsequent parliamentary appropriation.
This subject was before the parliamentary committee on railways and shipping. That committee has tabled its report. The findings of the committee are before the house. I would point out to hon. members that the report of the committee does not represent the unanimous opinion of the members thereof, and that other proposals which were not incorporated in the report were made in the committee. Since those proposals are not before us today I submit it is appropriate that they should now be placed before this committee and the government, so that when

we are considering a provision which says that the deficits shall be paid, we may at the same time suggest what should be done to limit such deficits to the lowest possible figure.
In addition to the recommendations contained in the report of the committee on railways and shipping on May 11, 1950, the following addition had been moved as an amendment to the report:
Your committee recommends that a uniform system should be adopted for the presentation of the accounts of the Canadian National Railways and Trans-Canada Air Lines, and that the consolidated balance sheet should show the accumulated surplus or deficit position in each case.
The vote taken on that occasion, may I add, was not one supported merely by members of the party to which I belong. However, the amendment was defeated by the close vote of eight to six.
Then another amendment was moved, suggesting that the following be added to the report:
Your committee recommends that an accounting system should be adopted which will make it possible to determine the profit or loss on each operating route.
On that motion the vote was even, seven to seven, with the chairman casting the deciding vote against the motion.
A further amendment was presented which proposed this as an addition to the report:
That the possibility of improvement in operating costs of Trans-Canada Air Lines be fully explored.
That was voted down. A further amendment was offered, that the following be added to the report:
That it is desirable to consider whether Trans-Canada Air Lines should be under the authority of the same minister as the Canadian National Railways, and also that the same minister who is responsible for the administration of the Aeronautics Act should have ministerial responsibility for Trans-Canada Air Lines.
That also was voted down, and, as in other cases I have mentioned, the amendment was supported not only by members of one party.
These motions, made for the purpose of adding these recommendations to the report of the committee which has been tabled, were directed to the one sound purpose in financial affairs, to giving parliament an opportunity to examine in a businesslike way this whole proposition so that, while Trans-Canada Air Lines might operate in the most efficient manner possible, steps should be taken, as they are taken in every large business, to examine its internal financial structure as well as its operating methods for the purpose of effecting any economies which might be made.
Canadian National Railways
Strangely enough, when it is suggested that there be economies in the operation of government enterprises, all too often we are met with the suggestion that an attempt is being made to limit the services rendered. The fact is that in any big business the services rendered are almost invariably increased by an examination such as that proposed in this instance. In fact it is the history of business that almost invariably where sensible and cautious steps of this kind are not taken, instead of expanding, the business will decrease in the extent of its operation, and ultimately, if that condition continues long enough without any effective internal examination of the kind here suggested, it will disappear.
When parliament takes the responsibility for setting up great publicly-owned enterprises it should be its responsibility also to require businesslike methods in dealing with them, so that the operations of such enterprises will be not only as efficient as they can be in the interests of the public, but also so that every practical economy may be practised to the end that, if possible, such economies may increase the general efficiency of the system in providing the service it purports to provide.
These proposals clearly reflect what was under consideration. The first part of the recommendation was that the report should contain a request that a uniform system should be adopted for the presentation of the accounts of Canadian National Railways and Trans-Canada Air Lines, and that the consolidated balance sheet should show the accumulated surplus or deficit position in each case. That proposal was made because the Trans-Canada Air Lines is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Canadian National Railways, and yet there is no uniform system of presenting accounts. In the examination of the accounts of the parent organization and of the subsidiary organization certain differences appear which do not make it as easy as it should be to examine the comparative statements.
It is desirable that there should be shown the accumulated surplus or deficit position. The reason for that is obvious, as those who sat on the committee will recall. I do not suggest that the accumulated deficit should become an additional part of the capital obligation, but it should be shown in the statement below the balance sheet so that those who examine the annual statement will know what the present position is as it has accumulated over the years.
When there were surpluses, those surpluses did accumulate and were carried in the annual statement. As those surpluses were exhausted by deficits, there should have

Canadian National Railways been carried forward a figure which would show the deficits so that those who examined the statement each year would be in a position to see exactly what the results of the operation had been.
When the time comes, as we hope it will, when there will be surpluses, it would not present an accurate picture of the long-term operation if the statement simply started in with a surplus and then the statements in future years showed the accumulation of surpluses. That would not represent the true operating position of the lines. One may ask: Why have these figures in there? They should be in there for the same reason that you have figures in the statement of any great operation of this kind which is owned by those who have invested their money in the ordinary way.

The report of that royal commission resulted in the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, which provided that deficits of the railways should be paid by parliament and not carried forward in railway accounts. The suggestion was made that separate accounting be provided for every route flown by the air lines. That was discussed in the committee. The comptroller of the Canadian National Railways, who is also comptroller of Trans-Canada Air Lines, explained that that procedure is not proper transportation accounting; that it was not the practice to make a separation of that kind in any transportation system with which he is acquainted. The president of Trans-Canada Air Lines pointed out that the cost of that type of accounting would be enormous, greatly exceeding the cost of accounting at present carried on; and that the results when obtained would be perfectly useless to the management. He pointed out that although a particular route may not be profitable in itself, it might very well be found profitable when its contribution to traffic on other routes is taken into consideration. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION FOR SAFETY OF LIFE AT SEA

speakeroldname: Hon. Lionel Chevrier (Minister of Transport) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION FOR SAFETY OF LIFE AT SEA
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 303, to amend the Canada Shipping Act, 1934.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION FOR SAFETY OF LIFE AT SEA
speechtext: Could we have a statement by the minister?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION FOR SAFETY OF LIFE AT SEA
speechtext:
The most important part of this bill deals with amendments to the Canada Shipping Act which are required in order to implement the international convention for the safety of life at sea, 1948, signed at London on June 10, 1948. The convention was signed by two of the Canadian delegates subject to acceptance, and the government proposes to accept the convention if and when parliament enacts the proposed amendments to the Canada Shipping Act contained in this bill.
It will be recalled that the safety convention of 1929 was made part of the law of Canada by the Safety of Life at Sea and Load Line Conventions Act of 1931. Subsequently, when the Canada Shipping Act, 1934, was passed, the safety convention was incorporated in that act as schedule 4, and the provisions of the act contain frequent references to the provisions of the 1929 convention. Consequently it is necessary to amend the Canada Shipping Act, 1934, in order to bring the provisions of that act in line with the new convention.
The safety convention of 1948 consists of fifteen articles. It is accompanied by six chapters of technical regulations which are difficult to paraphrase or summarize without affecting their significance. However, I shall endeavour to indicate in a general way the directions in which they differ from the 1929 convention. The convention itself has chiefly to do with the contractual relations between the governments which are parties to it. Throughout this convention the concept that there will come into being a permanent international wartime organization is followed. Article I contains the contract between governments to give effect to the convention by any necessary national action. Article II sets forth the ships to which the convention applies. Article III provides for an interchange of information between governments, and article IV deals with cases of force majeure. In general these articles differ little from the 1929 convention.

Articles V and VI contain provisions for deviation from the requirements of the convention in cases of emergency. Article VII abrogates the 1929 convention as between contracting governments.
Article IX provides for future amendments of the convention or of the regulations. All proposals for amendments submitted by member governments go to the maritime safety committee of the permanent international maritime organization known as the intergovernmental maritime consultative organization familiarly called IMCO, and are communicated by that organization to all contracting governments for their consideration at least six months before they are considered by the assembly. The assembly provided for in the IMCO convention is a meeting of representatives of the various member states, in effect an international diplomatic conference, meeting at fixed intervals of two years. These biennial meetings of the assembly afford a means of adopting needed amendments without long intervals, as in the case of ad hoc conferences. It should be noted that article IX differs from the 1929 provisions regarding amendments by requiring a screening by the maritime safety committee of IMCO; by requiring circulation at least six months in advance of consideration; by permitting consideration only at biennial meetings of the assembly, and by requiring a two-thirds majority vote of the assembly and of the maritime safety committee. There is a specific prohibition against making structural amendments retroactive. Generally speaking, article IX provides such machinery for the amendment of the convention as may be desirable, but surrounds such machinery with safeguards against hasty or ill-considered changes. A provision in article XV permits a conference to be called for amending the convention if IMCO is not in force.
Article XI provides that the convention is to come into force on January 1, 1951, if by January 1, 1950, fifteen governments, including at least seven governments having not less than one million gross tons of shipping have accepted it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION FOR SAFETY OF LIFE AT SEA
speechtext: Has that happened?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION FOR SAFETY OF LIFE AT SEA
speechtext:
No, as I will indicate in just a moment. Otherwise it will come into force one year after such fifteen governments have deposited their acceptances. At the present time-and now I deal with the question of the hon. member-I am advised that the convention has been accepted by the United Kingdom, the United States of America, the French republic, the Netherlands, New Zealand and Sweden. But as not enough acceptances were deposited before January 1, 1950, the convention will not come into force
Canada Shipping Act
on January 1, 1951. It will not come into force until accepted by fifteen governments.
I shall deal now with the chapters in the various regulations. Chapter I of the regulations contains general provisions as to their application. Unless expressly provided otherwise, the regulations apply only to ships engaged on international voyages. Regulation 3 excepts certain classes of ships such as troopships, warships, cargo ships of less than 500 tons gross, ships not propelled by mechanical means, yachts and fishing vessels. In addition, special exemption is given to vessels solely navigating the great lakes and the St. Lawrence river as far east as Montreal.
Regulations 6 to 19 inclusive of chapter I provide for the inspection and survey of ships subject to the convention, and for the issue and acceptance of certificates. These fourteen regulations follow generally the pattern laid down in the 1929 convention, but additional certificates have been provided to take care of new requirements. Regulation 20 has no counterpart in the 1929 convention. It specifically requires each government to conduct an investigation of any major marine casualty and to supply IMCO with pertinent information concerning such casualties, particularly where such information bears upon the operation of the regulations. This provision should result in the accumulation in a central body of valuable data for use in considering future amendments to the regulations.
Chapter II deals with the construction of ships from the safety standpoint, with special regard to the prevention or mitigation of casualties. New provisions are contained in this chapter requiring that a vessel shall have adequate stability when in a damaged condition. The convention considerably exceeds that of 1929 in its requirements for protection against fire. It authorizes three alternative approaches to the problem. The first is the essentially incombustible ship; the second depends upon an automatic sprinkler installation; and the third requires the extensive use of fire-retardant bulkheads together with the installation of an automatic fire-detection system. The adoption of regulations setting forth definite requirements for protection against fire is one of the outstanding features of the convention.
Basic regulations are included dealing with those electrical installations on passenger ships which are essential for safety. This subject was not dealt with in 1929, but the increased use of electricity since that time made its consideration imperative. In the

Canada Shipping Act
1929 convention it was provided that passenger ships should be inclined upon their completion, and the elements of their stability be made known to their operating personnel. The new convention extends this requirement to cargo ships of 500 gross tons and upwards. The convention also makes provision for fire-extinguishing appliances on cargo ships of 1,000 gross tons and upwards. The previous convention dealt in this respect with passenger ships only.
Chapter III deals with life-saving appliances and emergency musters and drills. A most important advance beyond the 1929 standards in this direction is the extension of many requirements to cargo ships of 500 tons and upwards. The definition of "short international voyage" is rewritten to include both length of voyage and distance off shore, and a measure of increased boatage is required for ships on such voyages.
Lifeboat equipment requirements have been increased in the light of lessons learned in the war. All lifeboats are required to be lifeboats of class I, and mechanical davits are required on ships over 150 feet in length.
All ships are required to carry means for making distress signals by day or night, and the line-throwing apparatus must now be capable of attaining a minimum range of 250 yards. The requirements as to musters and drills on board ship are increased, and in certain directions are made applicable to cargo ships.
Chapter IV covers radiotelegraphy and radiotelephony. This chapter requires cargo vessels of 500 gross tons and over, but under 1,600 gross tons, to be equipped with a radiotelephone installation if not fitted with a radiotelegraph installation. In the 1929 convention the minimum limit on cargo vessels was 1,600 gross tons, and there was then, and is now, no radiotelephone alternative for these larger ships. Chapter IV further provides for a greater degree of flexibility in permitting exemption from radio in that the exemption is not necessarily related to specific mileage, may be partial or conditional, and must take into account the various conditions surrounding the particular voyage.
The requirements of this chapter as to listening on distress frequencies, except for cargo ships of less than 1,600 gross tons, involve advances as to the hours of operatorlistening, and as to the installation and operation of auto alarms. The new provisions substantially increase the possibility of distress messages being promptly picked up by ship stations. The technical requirements as to radiotelegraph installations both on board

ship and for use in lifeboats represent a substantial advance over those contained in the 1929 convention.
The necessary changes in the requirements as to surveys and as to certificates have been made to suit the new provisions. A certificate called a safety radiotelephony certificate is established to cover the small cargo craft and conditionally exempted ships equipped with radiotelephone only. Provisions have been made so that the distress frequencies, to which reference is made in the new convention, shall follow any future requirements adopted by the international telecommunication union.
Chapter V deals with safety of navigation, under which broad term a number of requirements chiefly of an operational nature are included. The chapter generally applies to all ships on all voyages, including those specifically excepted by chapter I, saving only ships of war.
The provisions in regard to meteorological services have been rearranged and expanded to take into account the recommendations of the international meteorological organization.
The procedures covered by article 45 of the 1929 convention relating to distress messages have been modified to take into account the increased range of marine radio installations, and to extend rescue provisions to aircraft or survival craft. The proposed regulations adequately provide for the securing of assistance from other vessels, but are designed to avoid interfering unduly with ships not needed for the rendering of assistance. The requirement of direction finders on board ship has been extended to all ships of 1,600 gross tons and upwards, as compared to passenger ships only of 5,000 gross tons and upwards required by the 1929 convention. This requirement may be deferred for two years from the date the new convention comes into force. Exemption may be allowed in the case of vessels operating in regions where there are few or no radio beacons, but the value of the direction finders from the rescue standpoint must be taken into account. In this connection a new regulation requires governments to set up such aids to navigation, including electronic aids, as the volume of traffic along their coasts and the degree of risk demand. Similarly, a new regulation requires each government to maintain adequate rescue equipment along its coasts.
Another new regulation provides for a simplified and efficient system of signals between a stranded vessel and a rescue party on shore. This system is easily understood, and involves no elaborate equipment on the

vessel. A regulation covering safe pilot ladders is included to make the boarding of ships in open waters less hazardous.
Chapter VI deals with the carriage of dangerous cargoes, that is to say cargoes which are dangerous either from their inherent nature or from their liability to shift at sea. Specifically, the subject of grain cargoes is dealt with in some detail, and requirements for adequate shifting boards are provided. There are now in force in Canada regulations, made under the Canada Shipping Act, covering the carriage of dangerous goods and regulations covering the stowage of grain cargoes. I think I may say that all the changes made in the new convention are in the direction of increased safety and take into account the advances made in ship construction and seamanship since 1929.
There are other provisions in the bill, apart from the safety convention, which the government considers it advisable to enact at this time. I should like to deal briefly with those now.
For some years there has been a feeling in this country that a ship registered in Canada should be described in the act as a Canadian ship. Our ships are known on the seas and lakes as Canadian ships, and fly the national colours of Canada. It is out of date to use the cumbersome expression- "British ship registered in Canada", or "ship registered in Canada," and to bring the act in line with modern usage the bill provides that the expression "Canadian ship" will be substituted for the expressions "ship registered in Canada" and "British ship registered in Canada", wherever these latter expressions occur. At the same time Canadian ships will retain their status as British ships and continue to enjoy the rights and privileges usually accorded to British ships on the high seas and in all ports of the world. The change is one of terminology and does not affect the legal status of ships of Canadian registry. It should commend itself to all members interested in Canadian shipping.
There are amendments designed to enable Canadian consular officers, wherever possible, to take over duties and responsibilities now performed by British consular officers in connection with Canadian ships and seamen. At ports where there are no Canadian consular officers the British consular officers will continue to act for Canada under arrangements made with the United Kingdom government.
There are also amendments concerning the licensing requirements of small craft under ten tons registered tonnage. At present these small vessels are not required to be registered but under section 107 of the act ships
Canada Shipping Act
exempted from the provisions of part I relating to measurement and registration are required to take a licence from a chief officer of customs. The licensing requirements cover small motorboats and pleasure craft owned by Canadians but do not cover small craft owned by aliens. There are many such vessels maintained in Canada by United States citizens who have summer residences in this country, and it is desirable to have these motorboats and yachts licensed and marked for identification purposes so that in case of accident the owner can be easily located.
There is also a problem connected with small boats equipped with outboard motors which under a strict interpretation of the act are required to be licensed.
The bill provides that the governor in council may make regulations respecting the licensing for identification purposes of small vessels under ten tons registered tonnage maintained in Canada by aliens; the licensing of vessels equipped with outboard motors; the marking of licensed vessels; the exemption from the licensing requirements of certain vessels to take care of special cases; and the imposition of a penalty for failure to license and mark. In view of the increasing navigational hazards caused by small craft and the extensive use made of these vessels in different waters, it is considered advisable to deal with the problem by regulation rather than by statutory provision.
Representations have been made that parliament should enact a motorboat act along the lines of the motorboat act of the United States which applies to motorboats and certain other vessels not more than 65 feet in length. While this suggestion is receiving the attention of the officers of my department, the government does not propose, at this time, to introduce a bill covering the whole field of motorboat regulation. There is, however, provision in the bill to amend the Canada Shipping Act to permit the issuance of temporary certificates as master to persons qualified to take charge of motor vessels, not exceeding 65 feet in length, carrying passengers in an open cockpit, or in a cockpit which is covered by a light trunk cabin, and plying on the inland or minor waters of Canada within specified limits. This will permit the operation of large motorboats carrying passengers, such as the well-known tour boats in the waters of the Thousand islands, where the operators have local knowledge of the waters but do not hold a regular certificate as master or mate for inland or minor waters.
There are other miscellaneous amendments contained in the bill including amendments relating to the pilotage service and other matters which I do not propose to explain in

Canada Shipping Act
detail. These amendments have been recommended by my officers, who are familiar with the workings of the act, and are considered to be in the interests of the shipping industry. After the discussion of this bill has been terminated, I propose to move that it be sent to a committee for study. While the bill appears to be fairly lengthy on the surface, as hon. members who have it with them will observe, there are but sixty-three sections. The rest of it deals with the articles, the chapters, and the regulations, pretty much in the same fashion as did the safety of life at sea convention, 1929. That convention was approved by the house and was later made a part of the Canada Shipping Act. The same procedure is being sought at this time and I propose at a later stage to move that the act be sent to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines for study.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION FOR SAFETY OF LIFE AT SEA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that this bill is to be sent to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines there is no need for me to say much about it today. I hope, however, that in that committee it will be possible for us to get a detailed explanation of the various sections of the bill and also of the provisions of the international convention. As we all know the session is drawing to an end, and at this particular stage in a session it is always difficult to give careful consideration to any measure, i hope the minister will arrange to have his officials present before the committee and that we shall be given every facility for getting a thorough understanding of the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION FOR SAFETY OF LIFE AT SEA
speechtext: I give that assurance now.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO RATIFY INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION FOR SAFETY OF LIFE AT SEA
speechtext:
As I see it, there is little that is controversial about the bill but there are details which are of some importance, particularly to those Canadians who live on the St. Lawrence river, on the Atlantic coast or on the Pacific coast. I also hope that the opportunity will be given to such bodies as the labour unions, the shipping people, and the shipbuilding people to have representatives appear before this committee should they wish to do so. I should also like to ask that the radio operators be permitted to make representations before the committee. I know that on the Pacific coast they are much concerned about a trend toward cutting down the use of radiotelegraphy and replacing it by the radiotelephone. That is something that has given a good deal of concern to these radio operators and also to many of the general public who are interested in the safety of ships. The shipping companies of course look at the question more from the point of view of cutting down expenses, and I presume they would be in favour of having more radio-

telephones and fewer radiotelegraphers. But the question of safety of life is directly involved in the question, and I trust that it will be possible to hear representations from both sides, if they wish to appear.
It may also be wise to have representations from the pilots of Canada. I do not know to what extent they are worried about the amendments to the Canada Shipping Act which affect them; but if they are concerned about any of these amendments, they should be given the opportunity to appear before the committee.
The minister has said that once this bill has been passed by the house, Canada will accept officially the international convention for the safety of life at sea. The terms of that convention are a schedule to this particular bill, and I take it that the committee will be considering that convention in the same way that the committee on external affairs, a few days ago, considered the convention setting up the international meteorological organization. Mr. Chairman, it seems to me this discussion has not been altogether fair to the committee or to the minister who introduced it. I suggest that as far as Indians are concerned there are two classes of thought in Canada. There are those who would like to see the Indian given the same status, God help him, as the white man at the earliest possible opportunity. On the other hand there are those who would like to see the Indian kept where he is today. In between those two schools of thought is a large section of the population which does not seem to consider the Indians one way or the other. To those who take an active interest in the affairs of the Indians and wish to see their status raised to that of full citizenship as quickly as possible, compatible with the interests of the Indians themselves, I suggest that owing to the circumstances of the past hundred years this cannot be done overnight. I think everyone will admit that we could not just wipe out the Indian Act and everything it implies; so it has to be done gradually. Just because nothing has been done in all the years past is no reason to oppose some action being taken now.
However, the point I wish to make is not concerned with taxation or representation. I suggest that if you are going to throw the vote to anybody just like that, they will treat it with the same degree of respect and consideration with which, unfortunately, it is treated by a great many of us. We are given the vote as a matter of course when we reach the age of twenty-one. The figures in any election will show that in some parts of the country we do not attach much importance to this vote that came to us in that way. I have not the figures, but I would not mind betting-if it were parliamentary to bet- that the percentage of nationalized Canadians who make use of their vote is much higher than that of Canadians by birth. So if we are to give the Indians the vote, and if it is to have any value to them, they must realize that responsibilities go with it; that if they are to acquire the privileges we enjoy as white Canadians they must accept the responsibilities that go with them. Unfortunately for all of us, those responsibilities include the right to pay taxes.
I would not like to see this differentiation with respect to the Indians continue longer than is absolutely necessary. I suggested to some Indian friends of mine some time ago that it might be a good plan to adopt the system followed in New Zealand with respect to the Maoris; that is, give them all the vote and let them elect their own members to

Dominion Elections Act four or six seats. They promptly replied, "That is not what we want. That will perpetuate the discrimination. We want to vote on a par with you". Well, Mr. Chairman, they are not going to vote on a par with us if from the financial aspect we continue to regard them as wards of the country, incapable of paying taxes, which implies the inability to earn a living in competition with the rest of us. I do not think it is fair to the Indians who really want to vote to assume that they would like to take it all on the one hand and assume no responsibility on the other. I would suggest to you that those who would accept the vote, and would take that right without paying their taxes, are perhaps those Indians who have not yet reached a stage of citizenship where they are entitled to vote. It is absolutely unfair to say, as I believe the member for Simcoe North said, that this government is giving the Indian no voice in the affairs of the country. By this act this government is giving to every Indian the opportunity to exercise his voice in the affairs of the country if he wants to do so as a tax-paying citizen. It is a step in the right direction, and I am a bit surprised it has not been accepted in that spirit. I feel confident that the Indians in my district, who are socially far advanced, will put themselves in a position where they can vote and pay taxes.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I perhaps did not make the position clear in the short answer I made to the hon. member for Calgary West. The situation in the past has been this, that the Indians hot resident on the reserve could vote at the federal elections. The Indians on the reserve could not vote, except veterans and their wives. We start with that, and go back three or four years to the time when the Indian Act committee was sitting. A great many Indians and Indian organizations appeared before the committee, and discussed the desirability of having all Indians vote in the federal election. My recollection is that there were 74 different representations made by Indian groups, bands or associations. Of the seventy-four, forty-nine said they did not want the vote, and twenty-five said they did. Of course, a number of qualifications were expressed. Some said quite distinctly that they were not citizens of Canada, did not desire to be citizens, and would take no part in the affairs of the country if they were given the opportunity. Others said they might consider becoming citizens and exercising the vote if their treaty rights were upheld. Some were afraid their treaty rights would perhaps not be observed if they were brought under the ordinary rules which apply to all of us.
It must be remembered that the Indian Act, in order to protect the Indian from, shall we say, economic distress in the early days, has always exempted the Indian on the reserve from paying personal property tax and real estate tax. That provision is in the present Indian Act, and is continued in the Indian bill which was introduced two
Dominion Elections Act weeks ago. Now, having those things in mind, and desiring to assist the Indian to become a full citizen of Canada, the government concluded that it would be desirable to give all Indians the vote, but it was not desirable that they should retain the exemption from personal property tax which they now enjoy under the Indian Act. Under these conditions one, two or three courses could be adopted. We could eliminate the personal property exemption in the Indian Act, if we desired, and give the vote at the same time; we could give the vote and retain the personal property exemption; or we could do as we have done. We have left it with the Indian to make his choice. The first lesson in Canadian citizenship surely is that we should all be equal with regard to paying taxes. With that thought in mind, this amendment was drafted and the result will simply be this. As formerly, all Indians off reserves may vote. Indians on reserves may retain their personal property tax exemption if they desire it, by not waiving their exemption, and consequently not having the vote. But we would hope, and I think probably the result will be, that a large number of Indians will sign this waiver of exemption, because they realize that if they desire to have a voice in sending a representative to the House of Commons, who will in turn impose taxes on them, no doubt, they therefore should subject themselves to the same kind of taxation as every member of the house is at the present time obliged to do. It has often been said-and I think some of the hon. members opposite and perhaps some on this side have said it-that the Indian was a second-grade citizen at the moment. Without admitting that, I hope the house will understand that we are trying to make him an equal citizen; but I do not think we should go one step further and make him a preferred citizen as against all others in the community.
With respect to the Eskimo, the difference is not that which has been made by the hon. member. The Eskimo is being given the vote because, under some conditions, he has shown his ability to exercise that proper judgment which we would expect of an elector. He is not exempt from taxation, as the Indian is. If he were, we would remove that exemption in the same way as we are removing it with respect to the Indian. If an Eskimo is in receipt of income sufficient to pay the present income tax, he will pay it. There is no question about that. There is no exemption at all. If I have not made this clear, I am sorry; but I would think that the committee would agree with me that this is the first step toward bringing the Indian within the influence of parliament and to bringing

Dominion Elections Act parliament within the influence of the Indian: by giving the vote to the Indian on the reserve on precisely the same terms as other Canadians receive it.

speechtext: I think there is a point touched on by the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth (Mr. Charlton) which is not sufficiently clear in the remarks that have been made by the minister; and I am not suggesting for a moment that the minister is not seeking to make it clear. But this is not a case of giving certain Indians a special exemption as a favour. We must go back to why the Indians were exempted from income tax or from any other taxes with regard to anything that they earn on the reserve. The Indians gave up their ancient claims to rich and valuable lands and it was part of a treaty between the Indians as tribes and the government of Canada. Under those treaties the Indians gave up rights which they believed were real. In return the dominion government, as its part of the treaty obligation, undertook to provide certain reserved areas where the Indians could live; undertook to give the Indians certain annual payments, both in kind and in cash; and also exempted them from taxation on such earnings as they might make on those reserves.

The exemption which relates to taxes was the carrying forward of a principle which was inherent in the relationship. The very fact that it is an exemption in relation to what they earn on the reserves indicates that it was in relation to their position on the reserves which is a position created under those earlier rights.
No Indian is exempt in respect of any money he earns outside the reserve itself. There is a real reason why similar treaties were not made with the Eskimos. At the moment it is * difficult to imagine that the areas occupied by the Eskimos had a substantial land value. Conceivably, at some future time, minerals may be discovered in some of the Eskimo areas, although that has not yet happened so far as I know. But it was an entirely different type of country. The Indians were giving up rights in the parts of the country, to a very considerable extent, that were the most productive. The Eskimo's situation was different. It seems that in this particular case the Indian is called upon to pay on anything that he earns outside the reserve, without any waiver; and I can only feel that while no unfairness may have been intended, that is what is actually resulting from a proposal of this kind and that we are asking the Indians on the reserve to pay for


the right to vote. I do not think that is consistent with our whole approach to this situation and I therefore think that the motion that has been made to amend the section is in keeping with the history of this situation and with the broad approach to the problem.
