I think there is one satisfactory feature about the discussion here this afternoon, Mr. Speaker. This is the first time that I can remember that this topic has been the source of so much discussion on both sides of the house, and I think that is a good thing. Perhaps it stems from the work of the Indian affairs committee of a couple of years ago and the fact that we are going to enact, I hope, a much more progressive Indian Act than we have had heretofore.
Whatever may be said about the matter, I think there is a principle involved. That principle is that the inhabitants of this country, no matter of what colour, race or creed, should have the right to vote. I think that the amendment that has been proposed should be supported by the house at this time. I am greatly, in sympathy with one suggestion made by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite), that in the granting of the right to vote the house might consider Indian representation as such. I think that practice has worked out well in New Zealand, and I believe it would be a fine thing to have in this house Indian representation by people of their own who would put forward the claims of the Indians and assist this house in reaching a conclusion with regard to the Indian problem in this country. Of one thing I am convinced. Largely because the Indians had no vote, had no representation and therefore had no influence in this house, they have been neglected for a good many years. There is one other fear one might have, and that is that they might be subject to political manipulation and political influence. That is one danger in the present circumstances. But after all, those of us who have lived in this country for a long time know groups of people who came out, unfamiliar with Canadian citizenship, in the early years of this century, and who were subject to political influence and political manipulation for a time; but they grew out of that. While for a time perhaps it had a bad effect, yet in the long run the people who were given the franchise appreciated it and used it. They have become citizens interested in all aspects of our public life and today are not subject to the kind of influences that might be exercised on our Indian population at this time. Therefore I cannot believe that that danger, though it is there and might prove to be a

Mr. Chairman, as I rose I thought I heard a voice call "Carried". Apparently the owner of that voice had not heard from Annapolis-Kings. If the minister detects an undertone of confidence in my voice I am sure he will the more appreciate, in a kindly way, what I have to say.
Just before the dinner adjournment I indicated that I intended to speak on industrial relations at perhaps greater length than is my custom. On this, the first occasion on which any of us has had anything to say with respect to labour relations, I intend to review as best I can the progress and development in this important field, including a bit of history and dealing with the present position, and to examine what I regard as certain trends which in my judgment augur well for the future.
I believe it will assist our understanding of the problem if we are conscious to some extent of the history of these developments. It is within the memory of many of us in this committee, for example, as to when the first large labour federation was formed. For a great many years we have had craft unions, which have confined themselves to the business of particular crafts. The I.T.U. or typographical union is an example of this; and it continues, as do many others, as a craft union. But it seems to me interesting to recall that the American federation of labor, the first organization to gather under its wing many craft organizations, was formed in our own time, in the city of Chicago, by Samuel Gompers, a little Welshman less than five feet tall, who came to the United States as an immigrant. I am sure many of us have forgotten that the brother organization, the committee for industrial organization, did not come into being until a comparatively few years ago, in 1931 if my memory serves me correctly.

Supply-Labour
Two men had much to do with that organization. John L. Lewis had his united mine workers of America, which in the beginning had a membership engaged only in the craft of coal mining. That was the first union to extend its operations to the unionization of projects or industries on an industrial basis. By that I mean that in a coal mine in Canada today, all persons engaged in that industry belong to the united mine workers of America including the carpenters-and there are many in a mine-the drivers, the machinists, the tipple men, and so on. In British Columbia the organization extends to include also railway employees, because the company that owns the mines operates its own railway in the Nanaimo area.
It is of some interest historically that Mr. Lewis sent Philip Murray into the steel plants to organize that industry on the same basis, and Philip Murray became the first president of that second large labour organization, the congress of industrial organizations or, as it is commonly known, the C.I.O. It is also of passing but not great interest that Lewis later threw Philip Murray out of the united mine workers, the charge against him being dual unionism. In other words Murray, originally a member of the coal miners' organization, being sent out by the president of the miners to do a job of steel organization, then was expelled from the U.M.W. of A. because of dual unionism, the duality being the steelworkers and the coalminers. That organization had a tremendous growth and marks, I think, the greatest change within organized labour. I refer, of course, to the business of organizing in one union the various craftsmen engaged in carrying on the work of a particular industry.
In Canada we have two companion organizations. The C.C.L. is the child, or perhaps I should more properly dignify it by saying that the C.C.L. is a partner of the new organization in the United States, the C.I.O. That, within unionism itself, it seems to me indicates the greatest change that has taken place within those organizations.
Everyone will say, and certainly the newspapers do, that certain individuals have been given too much power; that may or may not be true. I think the man picked on most by commentators, editorialists, and so on, without complete knowledge on their part, is John L. Lewis. They have gone altogether too far, and made many charges against that man which are without justification. While realizing that the leader of the united mine workers has committed excesses, I am unable to forget the great elevation that he has given to his men and their families in matters of
IMr. Smith (Calgary West).]
daily living; and particularly in matters permitting the parents and children to receive a proper education which fitted them to go forth into the world, and take their part in the struggle for existence. Let no one think that I am condoning, for example, this simple fact: Within the last year or two that one man has held a nation, yes even a continent, in fear. It seems to me that is an example of absolute power perhaps growing and feeding on itself, and thus doing things which in a democracy we cannot condone. We are hoping the day -has gone when any individual controlling an organization of any kind can hold a continent in fear, and hold perhaps its future for a time at least in the hollow of his hand.
When I say that neither am I going to forget that industry itself, in that same period, was guilty of excesses. I do not think anyone in this House of Commons who had read Mr. McGregor's report on the bread-baking industry, the flour industry, the rubber industry or the glass industry, could for one moment say that in those cases industry has been altogether altruistic in its outlook. I believe that is true of some industries not yet examined. That brings us in these matters to the point where it is necessary that legislatures and parliaments take a hand, because only in legislatures and parliaments do we find a system of some control of excesses of this and other kinds. So we come back historically to this. Why have we organized labour? I have said before, and I repeat tonight, the reason is that, up to some years ago, industry regarded labour merely as an intake product. My reading of the history of the labour movement is that labour organized in self-defence. I am not suggesting for a moment that that was necessary, but I do say it was something which expedited the growth of unionism. So I now repeat what I said the first day that I came to this House of Commons: I believe in organized labour. I add that I believe in strong unions.
We all say here that we believe in collective bargaining. That is something which has been adopted in our own legislation, and in the legislation of every province in Canada. But, Mr. Chairman, we are speaking with our tongue in our cheek if we do not add that we believe in the bargaining between industry and strong unions, because without that collective bargaining has no meaning. There can be no proper collective bargaining except between equals or people who are nearly equal. The day has long since gone by when labour received something as a matter of generosity. Let me say this: I am sorry to say what I have because I know there are some institutions, large employers of labour, that are not unionized or being unionized. They have never had any difficulty. I think perhaps

one of the great examples on this continent is Lever Brothers, the largest manufacturers of soap on this continent. So that struggle, so to speak, was forced on a great many of our people simply by circumstance. But that which was at the bottom of labour organizations was the greatest circumstance in the world, enough to eat, a place to live in, and an opportunity to bring up a family, not in fear of starvation but with some opportunity.
We all say we should live in fear of God. How can that be done if you and your children are hungry? So, today we have reached a position where we have at least strong unions. I am going to say that I think that has gone as far as it should go. I know there are many people who, when they find difficulty in this or other civilized countries, say that there should be a law: "that should not be, we must have a law." Mr. Chairman, I want to make it plain that there are many things which law can do, but there are also many things which law simply cannot do. Take a simple illustration. You cannot make a woman sing, nor can you make a man work. All that law can do is to say if you do not do so and so, then you will be subject to certain penalties. That is the most that law can do anywhere. Leaving our legislation as general as possible along those lines seems to me the best method; and I intend to quote some cases which I think prove that we should have our industrial legislation in rather general terms.
At the present time we find labour well organized. What have been its gains? In numbers during the last war the gains have been tremendous. We find today labour organizations which until a few years ago were undreamed of. I give you as the best example the largest union on the North American continent, the automobile workers' union. I am glad to see the tremendous growth they have had, and before I have finished I intend to mention what I think is a great achievement of statesmanship between that union led by Walter Reuther and the General Motors Company, the largest employers of labour in the United States of America.
I want to make this fact plain. Labour properly began to raise wages. To do what? To get its share of the profit dollar of industry; because without the profit dollar there cannot be dividends and neither can there be wages. To me one of the most significant things happened just a few years ago where three men met. They were Eric Johnston, who was then president of the United States chamber of commerce; Philip Murray, the head of the C.I.O.; and Mr. Green, head of the A.F. of L. They gave us a seven-point program for progress in American industry.

Supply-Labour
But all three agreed and affirmed the profit motive in industry. We do not hear much of it lately-and you do not hear of it at all in the United States-but some people here, the C.I.O. for example, use this catch phrase: Production for use and not for pofit. Only in Canada on this continent do you hear anything of that. For a time in the United States, in election after election, Mr. Eugene Debs, the socialist candidate ran. He polled an insignificant number of votes. In late years it has been Mr. Thomas. But their polling of votes is so insignificant as not to be a factor in politics over there.
I mention that fact because they have affirmed the profit motive as the principle which makes industry tick and which therefore makes production grow, and without which we all know there can be neither money to pay wages nor money to pay dividends. In saying that I know that I am not asserting any new principle but am affirming an extremely old one. What does it mean? It means that both parties are entitled to a fair share of that profit dollar; but it also means that both parties must pull their oars in the production boat in order to entitle them to any share of that profit dollar.
We can all remember-and I am sure the minister remembers it well-that in the old days the great battle was based on an hourly wage or a daily wage. That is still true. I advised some people in labour with whom I was quite closely associated for some time that I thought they were wrong. I still think so. I am sorry to say that in these industrial matters we are still battling over so much an hour, so much a day or so much a week. It seems to me the principle which we must find, and we have not reached it yet, is one whereby the man who sells his labour can find some means of not eating roast beef when business is good and starving the rest of the time; surely we can find some system whereby that individual can eat with his family over twelve months of the year as long as there are twelve months in a year. I am not saying offhand that therefore any industry must provide a living-and by a living I do not mean an existence; I mean a decent living. All industries cannot provide those wages for a twelve-month period because having regard to climatic conditions, and having regard often to the product which is produced, we cannot bring everything to that basis. But it seems to me that the job of industry is this, and I include farming; I include every instrument from a spade to a tractor: the things which are produced. Without shifting labour all over the country when this industry closes or when that industry

Supply-Labour
closes, the nearer we can get to finding a twelve-month basis on which to obtain our labour forces, then, in my judgment, while we may not have reached the millennium, we have made an approach to it. We then will have laid the foundation for a lasting peace in industrial relations.
Speaking again of this profit dollar-a profit dollar in industry for whom? I give this thought to the house, not in any sense urging it strongly, but it seems to me we have advances to make on that basis. Surely industry and labour within itself can find some means of giving labour a greater portion of that profit dollar as profits increase instead of all of us being bound by this so much an hour, so much a day, so much a week business.
As to those of us who say in our economics that we believe in the profit motive, let us think:	Profit for whom? Let us have profit
for whom? Surely not only for the person who owns the plant. Surely we must in some way or other include those hundreds of thousands of people who are engaged in the operation of that plant, and I use the word "plant" in its broadest sense. Surely we must realize that they are part of the profit system; and, when justified by larger profits, they are entitled to a larger share of that profit dollar.
Now I come to this point. Some hardheaded people will tell me that I am theoretical, idealistic, that I am talking about something that I know nothing about. In answer to that I say this. The scheme in which I am so interested, not advocating, is a matter for study by this house and by those in authority in the department. It seems to me to be so important that we should raise our sights a little and not confine ourselves to the minimum way. We are now raising hourly wages in cents, and so on. Taking the long view we should seek a system whereby we will not have these uprisings and stirrings every month or so. We should endeavour to have the long view and get on a long basis.
I notice some people smiling; therefore I am going to give an example of progress in the very thing that I am talking about. I think the agreement arrived at the other day between the automobile workers and General Motors marks an important milestone in the history of negotiations, of settlement between labour and industry. It is too recent for anyone to have forgotten. The point I emphasize is this. It is a settlement on a five-year basis. After all the struggle and trouble that we have been through, to my

mind that is the finest trend-if it marks a trend, and I think it does-in the settlement of these relations.
I confess that General Motors must have a deep consciousness of conviction that things economically in the United States are not going to pot, that they are going to progress; because in the arrangements which they have made, aside from pension benefits or other benefits, they have arranged for an hourly increase in pay during the life of that agreement. But then, what do they get in return? They get peace; they get enthusiasm in their working force. In my judgment that is a tremendous advance in labour relations as we know them on this continent. I hope and I trust that that example may be followed in many other industries because we are arriving somewhere. But, Mr. Chairman, aside from all these material things, aside from picking this and that and the other thing out, I think what it has demonstrated above all is that it shows what can be accomplished. By whom? By men of good will. You will never get anywhere in these things as long as you have some individual who just says:	"They are all wrong about
that" and who sits there. I have seen some labour negotiations; and when I speak of this good will I bring it down in its application to something of which I have some knowledge.
I have seen this happen; in fact it nearly always happens. I know that, in contracts made by the industries in Alberta and in British Columbia with the united mine workers, it is going to take at least three days before they get anywhere. Everybody knows that. They meet the first day. One side states its ultimatum and the other side gives you its ultimatum, made a little tougher perhaps, because of what the first fellow has said. And then we all go home. Well, perhaps some of us do not go home. We may stay in the hotel or something of that kind. A buys B a cigar; C may buy D his dinner. Do not think that labour is broke any more. I am happy to know that they stay at the best hotels in the country, as they should. They stay in the same place as the people with whom they are negotiating. I would not suggest-
Where the farmers should be able to stay.
They go to California.

If I had the
opportunity I would ask you to drive me in your Packard to Florida, but at the moment I am not going to ask you to do that.
I would not go so far as to say that one might buy the other a Coca-Cola particularly if the hon. member for Fort William were

around. The point I am trying to make is that they know the kind of men with whom they are dealing-and there are some men with whom we cannot deal; do not let us have any doubt about that, but there is usually a way of taking care of them, because in these affairs it is a majority-rule matter, the old democratic way which is in vogue in this chamber. I have seen it happen so often. One side says: "I have read all sorts of things about that big shot. He is not such a bad fellow as I thought he was." Therefore this three-day rule in the coal business-and it is by custom a rule-is an excellent one, because by the time they get down to business and try to settle their contracts those engaged in the negotiations usually have come to the conclusion that their opposite numbers are human and are not such bad fellows after all. That is what conciliation is. That is why it is so wise that in practically all civilized countries we have come to rely on the help of conciliation. But again I repeat, sir, that conciliation can only take place between men of good will. Therefore it behooves all of us not to make snap or quick judgments when we read something in the paper about something that is happening in Tennessee, in the coal mines of West Virginia, in the theatres of Hollywood, and in the musicians' union somewhere else. Do not let us rush to conclusions. Before we make up our minds let us get both sides of the picture and hope that from then on negotations will be conducted by men of good will.
I intend to say a word about the future; and I intend to mention some trends through events that have happened in my own time which I think augur well for the future. I have already said, sir, that these organizations came into being in the time of many of us who are sitting in this house. But I am going to enumerate two or three things that have happened, and that is by legislation, in favour of labour. The first I mention is workmen's compensation which, I believe, is in all the provinces of Canada. The next is unemployment insurance. Let no one try to deny that those are advances on the humanitarian side of the problem I have been discussing.
Today in industrial organizations we have personnel men. Some of them are good and some of them, I know, are bad; the human factor never attains perfection. But only fifteen years ago who in this chamber this evening would have heard of a man's being paid money to act as a personnel man in dealing with employees?
We have many things of that kind. For instance, we have pension plans. There are between 600,000 and 700,000 labourers under such plans, if I remember correctly-
Supply-Labour
and I am proud of the word "labourer"; do not ever think that I am using that word in any sneering fashion. There are that many labourers who are taking advantage of industrial pension schemes which have developed as a result of agreement between themselves and their employers. In most cases both employer and employee make contributions to the funds thus set up which ultimately result in pensions for individuals.
Then there are thrift plans, savings plans, in many organizations today. None of us in this room ever heard of such schemes as far back as, let us say, fifteen years ago. So the point I am trying to make is that it seems to me industry has learned its lesson and now regards labour from the humanitarian standpoint, where formerly it did no such thing.
Let us take a look at labour-management committees. I know many of us think that those are grievance committees. They are not, at all. The minute a labour-management committee becomes a grievance committee it loses its usefulness. It is true that in all labour contracts today, or practically all of them, grievance procedure is set out. There are some difficulties in some industries as to when and where a man may consult his grievance officers-"grievance steward", I believe is the term used. I mention these things only to show the advances which have been made within the organizations themselves.
Now my time has expired.
Carry on.

May I mention one thing which I believe is of importance to all of us-and in this I pay the greatest possible compliment to organized labour that I am capable of paying. I refer to organized labour ridding itself of communist leadership. Mr. Chairman, that was not easy. Walter Reuther has only one useful arm today because of the job he did in that cause. Remember, it required not only moral but also physical courage. I wonder how many hon. members know the type of letters that fellows I know so well-Pat Conroy, for instance-have received when doing what he and his fellow officers have done in getting rid of men like Jackson, the head of the electrical workers in this country. It is no sissy business those men are engaged in.
You're telling me!

So far as I am
concerned, I hope none of us ever again, when the word "communism" is mentioned, will think of labour without remembering that organized labour has done more than any other agency, and done it more effectively, to stem the rust of communism in this country.

Supply-Labour
Let me refer to one other thing-and that only for a moment, because I know that today coal miners get good wages. I have been underground in many mines. So far as I am concerned, they cannot be paid too much; that is no place for me.
Today in the town of Cadomin there are five men, all of them with families, who are buried in the rocks and muck from a flash flood in the Cadomin mine. So, never again let us listen to anyone who says, "Oh, those so-and-so miners, they are getting $14 a day"-or they are getting this, that or the other thing. True, economically these things can and do get out of line. But let us never forget that today there are five widows and fifteen or twenty kids standing at the pithead at Cadomin waiting until the emaciated and smashed remains of their fathers and the providers for those families come to the surface.
Let us also not forget that in the town of Nordegg, where I personally have stood and counted the graves of thirty-nine men killed in the mine, the town is today burned out. I do not know how many were employed there -perhaps three or four hundred. But all there is in that town of Nordegg is the Brasseau mine, and the mine cannot possibly operate again for six months. So far as I am concerned, I hope those men have been paid enough money so that they can get by until the opportunity to work again comes to them. I hope they have been getting enough to make savings of that kind.
I close with this:	Having regard to the
ladder of progress I have mentioned, much of it as a result of legislative action by parliaments or legislatures, in the over-all picture I cannot help being optimistic. Anyone who has compared the present situation with what it was twenty-five years ago, and has not marked the improvement, must indeed be a pessimist. And so in this Dominion of Canada, sitting as we do on the finest resources left in this world, and with a good machine for employment, and with a strong and virile labouring force, and with humanitarianism at last in the minds of management, he must be a pessimist indeed who falters after looking at the bright sunshine which sheds its rays on our industrial Canada, and all men of good will engaged therein.

Mr. Chairman, I thought that we were intended to discuss the estimates of the Department of Labour tonight. I have never attempted to weary the house by holding a post mortem on the development of labour in Canada, tout after listening to the hon. member for Calgary West for the last hour my thoughts were provoked back

to matters that I like to forget. I am going to say a few words about the statement the hon. member has just made. If he reads it tomorrow I think he will find it rather difficult to know on which side he is. I was reminded of a lot of speeches made by the former prime minister. He would nearly say something in one paragraph, he would change it in the next and then he would finish up by not having said very much about anything.
One thing in the hon. member's remarks that stuck in my mind was the statement that all the advances in the field of labour in this country had been brought about by legislative means. With that I disagree completely. I can remember the efforts made to organize labour in this country for a long time back, and that was not as a payroller tout as one of the rank and file who can take some credit for the basic organization of labour.
When the hon. member makes a statement that we have gone a long way and that labour is well organized in this country, that statement is not correct. Out of a total potential trade union membership of five million there are only about two million workers organized. There are still three million unorganized workers in this country.
How many were there in 1939?

The basic organization of labour was not brought about by the legislatures or by this House of Commons. Unionism in its early days had no friends in the legislatures or in the House of Commons. The war periods gave labour the opportunity to organize. I can remember before the first war helping a lot of men, who never got their names in the newspapers, set up the basic organization of the mine workers union in Nova Scotia. They would allow you to fool around with the provincial machine that did not mean very much, but I can remember seeing Nova Scotia barb-wired in 1909 when the united mine workers attempted to come into that province for the purpose of setting up international unionism in Canada to replace the company organization that was functioning at that time.
I can remember sitting in a hall and seeing company stooges shoot potential union men for no other reason than that they were union men. I heard no protests at that time, either in the legislature or in the House of Commons. The people who did the shooting were never even tried. I can remember seeing women and children thrown out on the streets and having to live in tents or in the basements of churches for months and

months. Even after that struggle the union was denied the right of recognition by the operators in that province.
Our first break came during the war of 1914 to 1918. I can remember before 1914 that I was fired a dozen times because I had put my name on a card showing that I had joined an organization. That state of affairs existed in Nova Scotia in 1914 and 1915. During the war period the mine workers came in and in 1919 they were able to set up their organization and succeed in getting a contract and absorbing the provincial organization. We had no legislation then and we had no friends to speak for us, either in the legislature or in the House of Commons.
I can remember when the trade union was recognized by the operators, but we still had no legislation. It was not until 1925 that we had our first trade union act in that time which was forced through by the opposition. The then leader of the C.C.F. party, Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, sent a draft bill to Nova Scotia setting out what he thought a trade union act should be. I was president of one of the organizations and I can remember forming committees and bombarding the legislature on the eve of an election. The leader of the opposition introduced the bill into the legislature and the government could not afford to ignore it. They took the draft bill and amended it to include the check-off privileges.
The hon. member went on to say that we had unemployment insurance. When did we get it? We got it after a struggle of 25 years by those who were organized in this country. On the eve of the last war we got the Unemployment Insurance Act. Then the hon. member said that we have compensation, that it was handed to us on a plate. We got a compensation act in Nova Scotia in 1917, in the midst of a war.
We had ours in Ontario long before that.
I am referring to Nova Scotia because that is what I know about. The hon. member spoke about personnel management. We got that only in the last war.
From the government.
I am ready to give credit when credit is coming to you. You went along with it, you developed the mechanics, but we did not get it until the last war.
Was it not worth fighting for?

The hon. member did not do much fighting for it. The same thing applies to labour-management committees. I am not criticizing the government; I am simply answering the statements made, intentionally
Supply-Labour
or otherwise, by the hon. member for Calgary West, that all the progress in the field of labour relations in this country was handed to labour on a platter by the legislatures and the House of Commons.
No.

On a question of privilege, I know the hon. member would not misquote me intentionally. I never said anything of the kind. I said that various improvements had come about through legislation. I did not say that it was handed on a platter by anybody to anybody else. I gave the greatest credit in the world to union organization. I said also that they were forced into that position as a matter of defence and had made great strides. I know the hon. member would not deliberately misquote me but people are listening to him- he is worth listening to as a rule-and I know he would want to be correct.

'I have no intention of misquoting the hon. gentleman and I would not be saying what I am saying were it not for the fact that I think that anyone reading his speech in Hansard and knowing the history of labour and its struggles and sacrifices might be misled.
I will accept the judgment of the hon. member if he will read it.

I am concerned about the fact that we are becoming complacent; we think the job is done. As far as I am concerned, I do not want to wait for another war in order to get into trade unionism those three million workers who are still unorganized. I don't want to kid the unorganized of this country that the labour department is going to send out people to organize them, or that anyone from this House of Commons will go out and organize them. The machinery is there now to make that work much easier than it was in the past, and the job must be done by the men in the field themselves. Their struggle is much easier than when we formed the basic organizations in this country a good many years ago. But it seems to take a war to break the jam and develop ideas that should be developed during peacetime so the machinery will be available if and when an emergency should hit the country.
I could go on and talk about this matter for hours but I do not want to; I want to try to forget that period in the development of the labour movement in this country. It does not bring back pleasant memories to me. What I -really want to talk about tonight is the labour department, and first I want to tell the minister that he is not going to be

Supply-Labour
bothered much from this corner. In the first place the government sent the hon. member for Vancouver East to Geneva as an adviser on labour matters to the delegation that went there, and I compliment the minister on his judgment. He chose a man with very wide experience; but if he were here tonight he would be discussing these estimates. Another person who will not be here tonight is the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who is in the committee that is trying to write a social security program.
As to the labour department, in the first place I recognize that the minister has a very capable organization. At the present time, owing to the fact that since the end of the war the labour relations picture has changed considerably as far as the federal department is concerned in that jurisdiction has been handed back to the provinces, the department is relatively free with the exception of conciliation and those workers coming under the national labour code, so there is not the pressure that existed during the war period. Nevertheless I want to say a word or two on some things that have to do with the dominion and the provinces.
The first thing I want to talk about is the fact that unemployment is still a responsibility of the federal government. I am not going to talk about the whole of Canada. There are hon. members here from the rest of Canada who can bring to the minister's attention what they think is wrong in that field; or if everything is all right they should tell him so. In the maritime provinces we have a permanent unemployment situation that is bad. In putting out figures on unemployment the federal government say that if more than five per cent of the working population is unemployed it spells danger and something must be done about it. That is the target they have set; that is what they consider dangerous. In the maritime provinces today we have some 57,000 unemployed, which according to government figures recently released is approximately ten per cent of the available working population. So the situation is twice as bad as it should be, according to the government's own analysis of unemployment. The over-all average across the country is about seven per cent.
The problem in the maritime provinces, mind you, is not regional or seasonal. The situation is bad. To some extent it was relieved following the end of the war by an arrangement under which the department took workers from the mari times to the central provinces. During the past two years, however, there have been layoffs in Ontario and Quebec, and most of the people who
[Mr. Gillis.l
were moved to the central provinces have found their way back to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. That problem is -aggravated by the fact that thousands of young men and women are leaving school every year, and there is no possible chance of employment for them in that area. For the last twenty-five or thirty years the maritime provinces have sent an average of some fifteen thousand young people to the United States each year. That migration has been continuous over that period of time; it is still going on, and nothing is being done to change the situation.
I have heard a great deal of talk in the house about mechanization of the coal mines and steel plants. Mechanization does not relieve unemployment; it creates it. Every time you bring in a more perfect machine you step up production, lower costs and put more men and women on the street. If anyone thinks that mechanization of the steel plants and coal mines is going to relieve the unemployment problem in that area, he is wrong; it will increase it. It is difficult to find risk capital to go into that part of the country, but in the immediate post-war period the government did have a program. It tabled a white paper in the house in which it said it had ready and surveyed a shelf of public works in the different provinces, which would relieve the unemployment problem. Well, that public works program has been shelved. In my part of the country at least great hopes were placed on having the Canso bridge commenced this spring, but now I understand the provincial government has gone and thrown a monkey wrench into the machinery. The bridge was all mapped out; the plans were drawn for a 22-foot bridge. Then the provincial government decided it wanted a 24-foot bridge. That may be just an excuse-
The provincial government did no such thing. This dominion parliament decided that the national highway would have to be 24 feet wide.
I am not talking about the national highway; I am talking about the bridge across the strait of Canso.
That is part of the highway.

The Minister of Transport, for whom I have a good deal of respect and who I think is reasonably truthful, told the house in reply to a question I asked that as far as they were concerned the plans were drafted and the bridge was to be 22 feet wide. Now the provincial government have taken the position that they want a 24-foot bridge, and if that is the case the provincial government are the people who made the

decision. The Minister of Transport and the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond had better get together and decide who's who and what's what on that point.
I suppose the hon. member knows that when the Canso bridge is built it will be part of the national highway.
That makes no difference. The national highway is going to be four thousand miles long, and it is only one mile across the strait of Canso.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think this discussion is pretty far from the Department of Labour.

Well, that is a matter of interpretation. I am talking about unemployment; I am talking about the government's public works program, and pointing out to the minister that this project would have employed a' large number of people and [DOT]taken the edge off that unemployment problem. I am not blaming the minister, but the matter has been messed up somewhere between Halifax and the Department of Transport. It is the same government, or governments of the same complexion; nevertheless that problem is still there.
I mention that project because it was something specific to which the people were looking forward, but the federal government had plans for other projects. Now it has decided not to go ahead with any of those works. That is the point I am coming to, that as far as this government is concerned it is now the responsibility of the provincial and municipal governments to devise ways and means of relieving unemployment. Any hon. member from the maritimes who will make an honest analysis of that problem in his own riding will tell you that neither the municipalities nor the provincial governments have either the capital or the technical people to carry on that work. It cannot be done. The planning must be done by the federal government, and a large part of the financing done here. In view of the fact that that particular angle of unemployment relief in that part of the country has been shelved, I am suggesting now to the Minister of Labour that some means should be found of assisting the municipality in doing something for the permanently unemployed people until there are other opportunities for them. I cannot see anything there for them at the present time.
The minister's department did make a gesture by providing supplementary allowances under the Unemployment Insurance Act. For a few months that helped, but it has run out and these people are back where they started. Some of these men have been
Supply-Labour
idle for the last two years, and some even longer than that. Most of them are veterans of this war, and they have exhausted everything. The provincial government has a responsibility; there is no doubt about that. I wonder if the minister's department could not consult with the provincial government to see if something could not be done about the unemployment problem, either by going ahead with some of the public works projects or by extending the supplementary benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
The second matter I wish to bring to the minister's attention concerns the employment offices across this country. They handle the unemployment insurance, and register the unemployed. I do not think those offices are serving the purpose they could serve in the field of unemployment. For example, they register the unemployed. They have their qualifications, their trade, and know how long they have been unemployed. I believe that seniority should govern in this matter, and the person who has been unemployed the longest, with due regard to family status, should be placed first. If the offices had a directive to that effect, I believe it would be carried out. What happens is that there is work for twenty or thirty men in a certain place. There are perhaps three thousand unemployed, or perhaps if it is like the city of Sydney there are five thousand in that one city. Instead of the employer taking his employees from the office that knows the circumstances and qualifications of each man, political pressure from the outside sends in a list, and that is the way the thing is done. The employment office has not the right to say that this man has been unemployed the longest, has family obligations, and his unemployment insurance has run out, so he should be employed first. It is not done that way.

If my hon. friend would permit a question concerning this political pressure from the outside, I should like to know, if there is political pressure on the employment offices from the outside, whether it is by my friend's party or my party or anyone. 1 should like to know that.
The minister was probably in the house when I brought up the question specifically-
I am not being critical, you understand.

No, but I brought this matter up with the Minister of Transport. I pointed out to him that, instead of the contractor at the local Sydney airport getting his men through the employment office, the men who were hired on that particular job had to go to the defeated federal and provincial candidate and

Supply-Labour
get a slip before they could secure employment. I suggested at that time that the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Transport should get together to see that government contracts have a clause written into them giving preference to veterans and preventing any kind of political skulduggery. I think the minister knows, and I think every member of this house who has an unemployment insurance office in his riding knows, that that kind of thing does happen. I know it is not the policy of the minister's department, but until such time as the offices are given some kind of instructions, and there is cooperation with the employer, that sort of thing will create friction and raise a question in the minds of the men who are standing in the queue looking for a job. The matter is not handled as it should be.
I should like to say to the minister that, so far as I am concerned, I do not want any favours in this matter. I do not make any recommendations, but any time a person comes to me and I can help him in any way his politics are immaterial. As long as he has the qualifications, I shall help him. The man who is unemployed the longest, who has the greatest family responsibility, as long as he has the qualifications to handle the position which may be vacant, is the one who should be employed first. I do not want to see it done in any other way. The employer is not co-operating as he should, particularly in the community from which I come. I say that because I know. They do not go to the office to seek their employees. They just pick and choose as they like in that coal and steel industry. During the war your offices served a useful purpose. An employer sent in his requirements, and the office filled them. When the war was over the employers got back to what they considered normal. The offices are able to do an excellent job if they receive the co-operation of the employer.
Another matter I should like to mention, because these are provincial-federal matters, is the matter of vocational training. There was a good job done in that field during the war, and I know the minister had an excellent staff. Since the end of the war a fairly good job has been done. I know of two spots in Nova Scotia where schools were operated jointly by the federal and provincial governments. Within the last few months I have seen press statements, and I have received wires, to the effect that the school at North Sydney was to be closed. It was doing an excellent job, not only in training veterans for employment after the war but in taking the young unemployed and training them in certain trades and skills, such as carpenters, bricklayers, masons and that kind of thing. The school was doing a good job in turning

out fine tradesmen. My information is that within the last couple of months the federal government has withdrawn from that field. The provincial government takes the stand it is not going to maintain the school, so it is being closed. I suggest to the minister that those schools were doing excellent work. They are equipped, and good men were running them. For the small amount of money that it costs to keep those schools operating, I believe the closing of them should be reconsidered. From time to time I hear in the house, and I support it, about grants to universities; and how necessary it is to train everyone in the university. However, we shall want hewers of wood and drawers of water. If every one comes out of a university with a B.A. and wants a job with the government, or is a doctor or lawyer, there will be no one to exploit, so no one will have any money to pay these people.	.
If one goes to the unemployment offices in -many sections, one finds a queue of young people outside. In the office there is a long list of requests for bricklayers, carpenters, and plasterers, but these people standing outside cannot fill those positions. There is a need for vocational training. The minister has faith in vocational training, I know. Instead of leaving the field, we should be expanding it.
Another matter I wish to take up with the minister is the fact that during the war- when there is a war on we can do a lot of things, and do them quickly-the minister's department established something I considered a long step forward. He established an apprenticeship in the coal mines of Nova Scotia. For the short time that that apprenticeship worked, it did an excellent job. It was praised in the highest way by the miners themselves. Many people think that, to be a coal miner, all you have to be able to do is to shovel coal. Coal mining is something which requires highly technical skill. In the coal mines of Nova Scotia, for example, you have to serve three years of apprenticeship underground and write two fairly stiff examinations before you qualify as a coal miner. You have got to know a good deal about ventilation, compressed air, roof pressures, electricity and things of that kind. You cannot learn that overnight; and you can go down there in a mine without any previous training and get your neck broken quickly.
The regulations in the coal mines of Nova Scotia are stiff. The minister's department established something that I thought was looking a long way to the future in those mines when he set up that apprenticeship in the mines of Nova Scotia; a young fellow went from the surface with experts who trained him for six months in all of the technique

of coal mining, and they could qualify him in six months to write his first examination and get his first papers. It takes him eighteen months to do that under ordinary circumstances and under exceedingly dangerous circumstances. But in effect they set up a school underground, and they were doing an excellent job and turned out a good type of miner. The miners themselves were all for it. I think the company agreed that the production of coal on those school faces was paying off the costs of training the trainee. But again, as soon as the war was over, that whole scheme folded up and was withdrawn. I am suggesting to the minister that, under Bill No. 217, you are loaning to the Dominion Coal Company in Nova Scotia some $7,500,000 to mechanize and to electrify the underground workings in those old collieries. If you can spend $7 million or $7,500,000 on equipment alone, you should be able to provide this training. It is a new type of equipment also, and it is a type of equipment such as the men going into these mines from now on should be trained in before they go in. That is in the interest of production and it is in the interest of everybody. I am making this suggestion to the minister now. I know that all of his department, the deputy minister and others, who worked on the vocational training end of the thing were all for this kind of thing. I know that the deputy minister in 1946 and in part of 1947 worked on and with the miners' unions and the coal company in Nova Scotia trying to continue that type of trainee program, but in the aftermath of the war they struck some stumbling blocks. I think perhaps the greatest one came from the company themselves. I suggest that that matter be given further study because it is necessary and it is in the interests of the industry. I am just leaving that thought with the minister again. Having regard to the small amount of money that that sort of thing cost-because in the final analysis it was not costing the company anything; the production from those school faces more than offset the cost of the training that was allocated to them-I suggest to the minister that he might take another look at this point that I mention.
I think the employment offices could be more effective if they had the co-operation of the employer or were given directives to handle unemployment on the basis of the longest out of a job, with the greatest number in the family, and got away from this idea of favouritism that exists in many of the offices across the country.
I am sorry that I occupied this amount of time. I did not intend to; and I want to assure the hon. member for Calgary West
Supply-Labour
that I was not being critical of him. He just opened up a lot of old sores in my mind when he began to talk, and I like to forget the past, particularly that past, and look to the future.
Do they fire their shots? I was wondering about their skill.

No. They have their fire bosses. I think too that labour has grown up. I think that in the two congresses of labour in this country you have as fine a body as exists in any country. Their work is difficult. To advance is the big problem. I think we have made many strides forward in the last twenty-five years. They were not easy strides. They were exceedingly painful ones in the early days.
They were.

I think one of the best developments I have seen in the last few months has been the realization on the part of labour that they have nearly reached the saturation point in demands for wages and they are turning their attention to social security matters. But one of the longest steps forward was the signing of the long-term contract. I know that the miners in Nova Scotia always insisted on a one-year contract. I concluded a long time ago that it was not good for the simple reason that you spent about five months negotiating your agreement; by the time you got it signed up you had about six months to run and you were back into trouble again. It did not give the operator nor the union itself a chance to plan or to find out where they fitted in.
How true.

In this last contract they got around to signing for two years. Over in the United States I think some of the industries have signed up for five years. I think the long term is a desirable thing from now on. I am appreciative of all the things that have been done by the departments of labour since they have had in the legislatures and in the House of Commons a few people to prod them along. They are not doing a bad job. I know the minister's department well, section by section. I got in touch with them. I think he has an excellent department, but they are being held back. There are a lot of limitations that we ourselves place on them. We are not prepared to push them as far as most of them would like to go. I am sorry that I have occupied so much time. I shall reserve the rest for the minister's estimates.

I should like to say a word-

I have got to keep all this in my mind, Mr. Chairman, and I will not keep you long. I deeply appreciate what the hon. member for Calgary West has said and also what the hon. member for Cape Breton South has said. It is almost like a competition to settle who of the three of us is going to be the next Minister of Labour. I think that is all to the good. I was quite interested in the statement of the hon. member for Calgary West. I knew many actors in the labour drama on the North American continent and in Europe and I think among us all a great deal has been done. Do not let us take all the credit. There are a great many people outside the labour movement and inside it who have made the contribution that has been made to raise the social standards of the working people of this nation in the last thirty years. It is like planting an acorn. You do not get an oak the next day.
As I have often said in this house, a trade union agreement is based on character; it is not a legal document. But there are in my judgment certain fundamentals that govern the life of a nation, of a trade union or of an employer group. I think it was my good friend the hon. member for Calgary West who spoke of production for use instead of profit. I do not know whether any members of this committee have read "Das Kapital" by Marx. I think I could count on both hands all those in the Dominion of Canada who have read that book. They start out with the first volume and get tired before they get to the end of it. Even then, I think old Karl was a crackpot. He could not make a success of his own business. He could not support his own family; he was kicked out of every country in Europe. He had to go to the one free country, Great Britain, where he made the necessary studies to make that thing which was the bible of the Russian revolution. As to the point of the hon. member for Calgary West on the profit urge, the wages of profit, the salaries of profit, even some of the members of the House of Commons have said to me, "I think we should get a bigger sessional indemnity." I mean, that is a natural thing.
Let us form a union.

It is why the birds go south in the winter and north in the summer. It is just as simple as that. I was in Russia when they were paying 10 per cent on deposits and 10 per cent on government bonds. You talk about risk capital. One of the fundamental principles of Lenin was: Destroy the currency of a nation and a revolution is just around the corner. He went out

and did that deliberately, with the result that in order to build up their comparatively small industrial structure they had to start afresh. There is nothing new about that. They were paying that much interest to get people to save money.
Let me say this, Mr. Chairman. I am from the working class. When you destroy the middle classes of a nation you are down the drain. I am not underestimating the contribution of many of the people who have spoken this evening, particularly my good friend, the hon. member for Cape Breton South, who was never a salaried employee of a trade union. He made his sacrifice and contribution to the miners in the maritime provinces. I have watched you struggle with your first union, and then your communist union and all that sort of thing down there until you got the powerful organization that you have today. I can say this also. You are one of the few districts in the united mine workers of America-probably the only one-where they still have democracy.
The hon. member for Calgary West was talking about John L. Lewis, who has made his contribution. What I like about Mr. Lewis is this. If it is yes, it is yes; if it is no, it is no. When he makes a contract he keeps it, with all his faults. However, I question the industrial statesmanship of any individual- and I am not speaking of any individual in particular at the moment-who can point a gun at a nation and get away with it, whether he be an employer or an employee. Lewis once said: "I cannot do anything with these Nova Scotia miners; they are democrats and Scotsmen; at least they claim to be." That is the later generation.
I am not going into the historical background, as the hon. member for Calgary West and the hon. member for Cape Breton South did, but there are certain things that I think we should remember. They are, bad money drives out good; money is timid; the law of diminishing returns, and don't be afraid of the machine. They are simple things; too simple. They like to make them complicated. There are four or five books in that sentence.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South talked about the machine. Not so long ago I was in one of the colonies. I do not like the word "colony." The governor asked me if I would meet the leader of the trade union congress there, which I did. I said: "What is your problem here?" He said: "They are introducing the bulldozer and the steam-shovel to build roads." I said: "What is wrong with that?" He said: "It will create unemployment." I said:	"What are you
doing now. How do you build your roads

now?" He said: "With wheelbarrows, pickaxes and shovels." I said: "Why not be logical and build with knives, forks and spoons, and you will all be rich." I said: "I come from a nation of 13 million people. It is not a country in the sense that most countries are countries; it is a continent, and we spanned that continent with steel and communications. We built schools, a judicial system and all these things that are so necessary to a civilized country and we let the machines do the work."
I can remember the day, I am sure most of us can, when I would not be wearing a union made suit like the one I have on at the present time which was made by Dave Dunkleman, an old friend of mine. I knew him as a worker in the trade. I paid $27.50 for this suit ten years ago, and it was made in a union shop with union help; but they could not have done it without the machine. Do not be afraid of the machine. Let the machine do the work. That is one of the reasons why we have such a high standard of living in the Dominion of Canada.
You have two suits a year, now.
Oh, yes. The best things in life are free. You know that. My hon. friend talked about-
The second suit is free.
Oh, no. My hon. friend talked about the government not sending out labour organizers. That is what they did in Russia.
I said I do not expect them to.

Let me say this clearly and with all the emphasis at my command. I am not suggesting that my hon. friend is following that kind of line; I have known him too long for that. But that was the implication in my hon. friend's remarks. In Russia of course the government runs the trade unions. They are the servants of the state. They are not free men as they are in North America. And that applies to other countries, and democratic countries, where the government calls the tune, where the trade union organizations are servants of the state. That was where the late Sam Gompers, whom my hon. friend talked about, showed more sense than any of them. He said: "Any trade union that gets tied up with a political organization will always live to regret the day that it got tied up with that organization."
You are asking for trouble right now.

I listened to my hon. friend. I say any political organization. I speak of
Supply-Labour
this party, the Social Credit party, and also the C.C.F. party. I believe in freedom. It is like the air you breathe. You do not miss it until it gets scarce. Do not let it get scarce.
There is another point, namely, seniority in connection with employment offices. Well, I always thought that an individual had the right to quit a job; that an employer had the right to fire a man. To me that is fundamental. The right to strike is fundamental; and that is implied in the employment offices. I like to go to whatever store I want to go to, to buy a pair of shoes, a hat or anything else. I do not think that my organization should tell an employer whom he should employ, or by the same token that my organization should tell an individual to take a job when he does not want to take that job. To me that is elementary and fundamental.
I believe the employment service should be based on service, service to the people of this nation. I often say to my people in the employment service: "It is only by the grace of God that you are not on the other side of the table." I say, "You may be the person who is out of work."
I deeply appreciate what both the previous speakers said about the organization in this department. I think that among us-I am not speaking in a party sense now, you understand-we have probably done as much in the last ten or fifteen years in this country as has been done by any other nation in a like period of time in furthering the interests of the great mass of people, whether they be agricultural, commercial or industrial, in the Dominion of Canada.
That was one point that was raised. The other was apprenticeship. In connection with apprenticeship, Mr. Chairman, I cannot quarrel with anything that has been said. I believe in it. The woods are full of Ph.D.'s and B.A.'s; but someone has to do the work. If you could erect buildings by making speeches I am certain that we could have erected many buildings in this House of Commons in the last three or four months. But you must have bricklayers, carpenters, plasterers, and so on all down the line, just as you must have miners. I speak now of what the hon. member for Calgary West said about miners. It is a difficult job to undertake. The dangers are great; the risks are great. I am a great believer in paying for the risk you take in an industry.
I want to say this very frankly if I may. I do not know whether it is safe to say this, but if I had to choose between being a lawyer and a bricklayer today, I would be a bricklayer.

Supply-Labour
Much better pay.

I would like to pay a tribute to a man-I do not often mention people's names in the House of Commons, or friends- in connection with the establishment of apprenticeship in Canada. One is Joseph Pigott of Hamilton, the contractor, another is the late Jim Marsh, and another the late Tom Moore, who laid the foundation of understanding with the provinces in connection with the establishment of the apprenticeship system in Canada. It is true that in this day and age people do not go in for the trades, as they did when I was a young man, or when my hon. friend was a young man in Nova Scotia. There does not seem to be the urge to do it today that there was when we were younger.
The machine has taken over; tradesmen are going out.
I cannot see that point of view, I am frank to admit. We have more machines; let the machines do the work.
Two pairs of pants.
And we have more suits, as my hon. friend from Simcoe North points out.
The two-pairs-of-pants county.

Absolutely. I am all for the machines. I remember when I was very closely associated with Sir Adam Beck in connection with the establishment of hydro in Ontario. They said, "You will never sell the power." It is true that Sir Adam tried to sell the power on every occasion, when we built at Queenston-but within three years there was a shortage.
The reason we enjoy this high standard of living in North America-and I am not going into figures-is because of the substitution of the machine for human labour. We cannot have a forty-hour week without the machine; let us be sensible about that. To my mind electrification is an elementary step. I would like to think that some of the countries in Europe and Asia had some of the advantages enjoyed by even the most lowly person-and I am not using that expression disrespectfully-in this country today.
About vocational training-

I spoke about the machine in its relationship to unemployment. It is all right to talk about a high standard of living but 57,000 people unemployed in the maritime provinces have a pretty low standard of living, while the machine produces the profits. What are you going to do with
57,000	unemployed in the maritimes?
tMr. Mitchell.]
It is not true; it is 13,000.*
The figure changes-

Of course they do. They are like the tides that rise and fall. Of course they change. Unemployment figures dropped over 100,000 in the last few weeks. You cannot pass laws in this House of Commons to stop the flooding of the Red river in Manitoba. Of course, they might promise to do that. You cannot pass laws to stop the flooding of the Fraser river. That is the only thing that has not been promised. Neither can we pass laws to change the weather. If you have a late season in British Columbia we all know it creates inescapable unemployment conditions. And so on, right 'across Canada. That was one of the reasons we established unemployment insurance-so ' that it would act as a cushion against that form of unemployment. I think probably we planned better than we knew. I am not taking credit for this party or government, although we did place that legislation on the statute books.
We live in a seasonal country where we are bound to have big shifts in employment in different seasons. I know that during the war, when I was in charge of manpower, I insisted that the farmers of this nation either put on uniforms or go into basic industries in the winter months. That worked out very well; most of them, I suppose, went into basic industries. However, that is beside the point.
When one talks about unemployment he must take that into account. He must remember that this is a cold and variable climate, and in the very nature of things we shall have ebbs and flows in unemployment conditions in Canada.
I agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South in the matter of vocational training. It was established while I was minister. We trained 650,000 for war industry to supply the army and navy during the war, and we have trained many thousands since, on a co-operative basis with the provinces and municipalities. I hope we may continue to do that. I shall be glad to look into the situation in North Sydney about which the hon. member spoke. It is obvious that I do not know every community in Canada, but I do have a fair understanding of the general policy of my department and its relationship to provincial government and municipalities in that connection.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to keep the committee long, but I must say a few words on this subject. First of all let me say that in my opinion the Minister

of Labour has done an excellent job in creating the machinery in Canada to a point where it has resulted in less labour and industrial strikes than anywhere else on the North American continent. For that he is to be commended.
However, there is a problem in connection with unemployment which members of the House of Commons appear to have overlooked. It is not long ago that we had about
420,000	unemployed in this country. That becomes a serious problem. It may be said that part of that was seasonal-and that would be true. But it is not going to remain a seasonal problem so long as we have such numbers as that. A portion of them will be more or less permanently unemployed.
It is my view that the federal government will have to take some responsibility for the maintenance and care of the employable unemployed. I do not believe the provinces are ever going to be in a position financially or otherwise, where they will be able to take care of any large-scale unemployment problems.
Only a few weeks ago I received word that in my own constituency there were 1,400 unemployed in the Drumheller coal-mining area. Coal-mining possibilities in western Canada are not as good as they used to be. Particularly since the war it is becoming more difficult to ship coal to eastern Canada so as to compete with coal coming in from the United States. We still ship in millions of tons from the United States, at a time when we have thousands of miners unemployed in this country. I suggest that the minister could assist the provinces in taking care of employable unemployed by establishing a national coal policy for Canada.
It is not my intention at this time to discuss a national coal policy, but it does seem to me somewhat ridiculous when we are so dependent upon the production of coal that we should allow that industry to deteriorate. In wartime Canada is dependent upon her coal industry being able and ready at all times to take care of the tremendous problems we are called upon to face in a time of emergency. It seems to me we should be doing everything possible to maintain that industry.
I suggest it is ridiculous that we should be importing millions of tons of coal when we have thousands of unemployed coal miners across the length and breadth of this country. In my judgment the provinces are not going to be able to take care of this problem. Alberta has been doing everything it could to build up industry within that province. The other western provinces and the maritimes are doing the same. For some reason or other
Supply-Labour
industry has been negligent-I use that word advisedly-in establishing itself in the two extreme parts of this dominion. It was my contention during the war, as it is yet, that we missed a great opportunity in not spreading our industry throughout the western provinces and the maritimes in order to take up this problem of unemployment in peacetime. Instead of that we concentrated all our industrial efforts in central Canada and that is where they have remained.
It is going to be exceedingly difficult to develop industry in the maritime provinces and the prairie provinces in view of the tremendous increase in freight rates just passed, some 45 per cent. Because of those increased freight rates an industrial barrier and tariff wall has been built around those provinces to make it impossible for us in the west to produce industrially and ship to the other provinces. This is going to present itself as a problem to the Minister of Labour when it is necessary to take care of the unemployed. I do not see how he can expect the provinces to carry this great burden on their shoulders.
It is true that at the present time the building industry in western Canada is absorbing a fairly large number of workers but we must remember that the building going on there is mainly the result of government financing under the national housing plan. There is comparatively little private building going on. And that is not a healthy sign, particularly in peacetime. Sooner or later the government is going to have to get out of the building business and when that happens there will be a tremendous drop in employment and our unemployment problem is going to be magnified to that extent.
In the past agriculture has been able to absorb a great many workers, particularly in harvest and seeding times, but agriculture has improved its methods and does not now require as many people to take off the crop. A moment ago the minister said that the modern machines are not displacing labour, but I think that is debatable. Certainly in the field of agriculture the modern machines which have been introduced have definitely decreased the number of employees. There used to be 15 or 20 men in a threshing crew but today the farmer and his son are able to do the whole operation.
The question today is: What are you going to do with the men who are being displaced by these machines? That is a problem we are going to have to face. They are going to have the same problem in the coal mines of western Canada as they have in Nova Scotia. What are you going to do with the men being displaced by modern machines?

I believe I could answer that question very effectively if the Chairman would allow me to explain the principles of Social Credit, but I know he would stop me and I shall leave that for another occasion.
Spare us.

I hear an hon. member say, *"Spare us". If he can get up and tell us how he is going, to take care of the unemployed I shall be glad to have him do so. I am afraid that in British Columbia they are going to be faced with the same difficulty of taking care of men who are being displaced by the modern machines of today. In industry all across the country you find that problem. As I say, the Department of Labour is going to have to face that problem sooner or later.
It might be said that it can be solved by increasing family allowances. The Liberal party does not laugh at family allowances today, but the fact is that it was only after having been pressed to adopt them by the Social Crediters that they introduced family allowances. I congratulate the government on having had that much wisdom. Another thing causing trouble today for the unemployed is the high taxation being imposed upon the people by the federal government. This is not the fault of the Department of Labour particularly, but they must bear some of that responsibility. That problem is going to become more magnified as time goes on.
It is all right to say that unemployment insurance is going to bridge the gap or that the supplementary payments that were introduced will help, but they were never intended to take care of permanent unemployed or employable unemployed. As the minister explained a few minutes ago, they are intended only to bridge the gap in seasonal unemployment. When you have five per cent cf your total labour force unemployed you have not a temporary or a seasonal problem, you have a permanent problem on your hands. When we have in the neighbourhood of
400,000	unemployed as we had a while ago- the figure is down now-that comes close to being what could be classed as a serious problem.
It is not my intention at this time to deal with some of the difficulties that face the unemployed people of Canada, because I could speak for an hour on that alone. In the discussion of the items we are given an opportunity to indicate how these problems may be solved and without keeping the committee any longer I shall conclude and save the rest of my remarks for the items.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think the hon. member for Calgary West is quite aware of the fact that the hon. member for Cape Breton South was handed a piece of paper on which were the results of the recent by-elections. When he saw the success of his party in those by-elections it probably accounted for his misinterpretation of the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary West.
As an employer of labour I want to say to the minister that he and his department should leave no stone unturned in drawing to the attention of employers the advantages of sharing the profits of industry with labour and of making working conditions as attractive as possible. In my factory I find that when a man has been imbibing a little too freely the night before and brings a big head to the breakfast the old woman has got for him in the morning he finds he does not feel like doing anything. But if that man is able to get a cup of coffee and a sandwich at a cafeteria around ten o'clock he does good work from that time until twelve o'clock. When plants are made attractive with beautiful lawns and flower beds and when they have facilities such as cafeterias there is greater inducement for labour to work. The labouring man finds that he wants to do a better job when he is employed in a plant of that type. I believe the department could point out to management the benefits which accrue when working conditions are improved, and I am sure any such suggestions would be gladly adopted, to the benefit of both the employer and the employee. Some years ago the factories of Canada were not fit for pigs to live in, let alone for men to work in; but for any labour man to suggest that the improvement in working conditions has been brought about entirely through the efforts of the unions is ridiculous. No one can really believe that all employers are heartless. We know they have been scratching their heads and racking their brains for years, figuring ways to co-operate with the employees and improve their conditions.

With the cost of a suit of clothes made without machines, one would have to make it last for seventeen years in order to get his money out of it. We should encourage the development of machinery, the improvement of what we have and the creation of new machines so people may better enjoy the fruits of their labour and the productivity of this country. We may have to reduce the hours of work of

the individual. That will be a godsend if it can be done. Let us never try to stop the development of new machines, for each new machine creates work that will increase the privileges enjoyed by all classes in our country.

I want to take only about three minutes to mention one specific matter. I brought it up last year and the minister could not see it, so I suppose he will not see it again this year. Nevertheless, at the request of the city council of Moose Jaw I am going to bring it to his attention again.
During the present session I have heard hon. members of all parties point out that unemployment is perhaps our major domestic problem, and I am inclined to agree. I want to lay one aspect of that problem before the minister tonight; that is the effect unemployment is having on municipal councils throughout the country. As has been pointed out already, a short time ago the number of unemployed passed the four hundred thousand mark. That is getting pretty high. Municipali-ities are viewing the situation with grave concern, because today the federal government pays no share of relief costs. Because of that fact many municipalities closed their financial books in 1949 with deficits for the first time in many years.
As city aldermen, reeves, mayors and others look at this problem they cannot help recalling the difficult times they had in the last depression, and wondering whether or not they were going to be faced with the same difficulties in the near future. In my own city of Moose Jaw just before the war, for instance, six thousand people out of twenty thousand were on direct relief. That was a strain which in large part had to be borne by the city council. During the last few years, because of the war, the revenues of the municipalities have been fairly buoyant and they have managed to get in better condition; but they are still in no better shape to meet heavy relief costs today than they were during the depression years. I know the minister will reply at once that since that time we have brought in the Unemployment Insurance Act, which of course I admit. But that legislation has shortcomings. It does not cover everyone; the period of benefits is limited; and because of the high cost of living many people receiving those benefits cannot get along on them. As a result the welfare organizations and municipal councils are having to bear a heavy share of relief costs.
As I said a moment ago, I pointed out this situation last December. At that time there were about 220,000 unemployed in the country, and I remember the minister rather
